cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of an option's historical volatility, measured across successive trading days, for a series of options with different expiration dates.
cards.explanation: A volatility smile uses forward-looking implied volatility backed out of traded prices, not backward-looking historical volatility, and it varies strike while holding maturity fixed.
cards.originalText: The plot of an option's historical volatility, measured across successive trading days, for a series of options with different expiration dates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
cards.explanation: A volatility smile plots implied volatility on the vertical axis against strike on the horizontal axis, with maturity held fixed.
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.
cards.explanation: Holding strike fixed and varying maturity gives the volatility term structure. The smile holds maturity fixed and varies strike.
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.
cards.correction: A volatility term structure is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility term structure is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given strike price, as a function of its time to maturity.
cards.explanation: Holding strike fixed and varying maturity gives the volatility term structure. The smile holds maturity fixed and varies strike.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the market price of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
cards.explanation: Plotting market price against strike gives the price curve. The smile plots the implied volatility backed out of those prices, not the prices themselves.
cards.originalText: The plot of the market price of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
cards.correction: An option price curve is the plot of the market price of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: An option price curve is the plot of the market price of an option with a given time to maturity, as a function of its strike price.
cards.explanation: Plotting market price against strike gives the price curve. The smile plots the implied volatility backed out of those prices, not the prices themselves.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: The implied volatility shape consistent with the lognormal price distribution assumed by BSM is a flat, horizontal line, because a single constant volatility prices every strike correctly.
cards.explanation: BSM assumes constant volatility and a lognormal terminal price, so one volatility would price every strike correctly and the implied volatility curve would be horizontal. Any smile or skew is a departure from BSM.
cards.originalText: A flat, horizontal line, because a single constant volatility prices every strike correctly.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical, because put-call parity forces the dollar pricing error of the model to be the same for both options.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity holds for both model and market prices, so the dollar pricing error on the call equals that on the put. Since price is strictly increasing in volatility, the same volatility zeroes both errors.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities are identical, because put-call parity forces the dollar pricing error of the model to be the same for both options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities differ, because a put's payoff is bounded above while a call's payoff is unbounded.
cards.explanation: Payoff asymmetry affects the price levels of calls and puts, but put-call parity forces their implied volatilities to be equal at a common strike and maturity.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities differ, because a put's payoff is bounded above while a call's payoff is unbounded.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical only when both options are at the money.
cards.explanation: Equality of call and put implied volatilities at a common strike and maturity holds at every strike, not only at the money, which is why calls and puts share a single smile.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities are identical only when both options are at the money.
cards.correction: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical whether or not both options are at the money.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical whether or not both options are at the money.
cards.explanation: Equality of call and put implied volatilities at a common strike and maturity holds at every strike, not only at the money, which is why calls and puts share a single smile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical only if the underlying price distribution is genuinely lognormal.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity is distribution-free, so call and put implied volatilities coincide even when the lognormal assumption fails.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities are identical only if the underlying price distribution is genuinely lognormal.
cards.correction: For a European call and a European put with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatilities are identical even if the underlying price distribution is not genuinely lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: Different implied volatilities for a European call and a European put at the same strike and maturity are a normal feature of the volatility surface.
cards.explanation: Implied volatility varies across strikes and maturities, but it cannot differ between a European call and put sharing the same strike and maturity. A difference signals a put-call parity violation and an arbitrage opportunity.
cards.originalText: No trade. Different implied volatilities for a call and a put at the same strike and maturity are a normal feature of the volatility surface.
cards.correction: Different implied volatilities for a European call and a European put at different strikes and maturities are a normal feature of the volatility surface.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: Different implied volatilities for a European call and a European put at different strikes and maturities are a normal feature of the volatility surface.
cards.explanation: Implied volatility varies across strikes and maturities, but it cannot differ between a European call and put sharing the same strike and maturity. A difference signals a put-call parity violation and an arbitrage opportunity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a symmetric smile.
cards.explanation: A platykurtic (light-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts cheap relative to BSM and produces a frown, not a smile.
cards.correction: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a frown.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A platykurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis below 3, produces a frown.
cards.explanation: A platykurtic (light-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts cheap relative to BSM and produces a frown, not a smile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces an inverted smile, or frown.
cards.explanation: A leptokurtic (heavy-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts expensive relative to BSM and produces a smile, not a frown.
cards.correction: A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces a smile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A leptokurtic implied log return distribution, with kurtosis above 3, produces a smile.
cards.explanation: A leptokurtic (heavy-tailed) implied log return distribution makes deep in- and out-of-the-money contracts expensive relative to BSM and produces a smile, not a frown.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A normal mixture implied log return distribution produces a frown, because mixing two normal distributions reduces kurtosis below 3.
cards.explanation: A normal mixture has kurtosis above 3, so it has heavy tails and produces a smile rather than a frown.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: A platykurtic implied log return distribution produces a frown, in which at-the-money options carry a higher implied volatility than both deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options.
cards.explanation: Light tails make deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money contracts worth less than BSM implies, depressing both wings and leaving the at-the-money implied volatility highest, which is a frown.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Event-driven hedge funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money call options on takeover candidates is likely to steepen the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.
cards.explanation: Out-of-the-money calls sit at high strikes, so extra demand for them lifts the right side of the curve and flattens rather than steepens the downward skew.
cards.originalText: Event-driven hedge funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money call options on takeover candidates.
cards.correction: Event-driven hedge funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money call options on takeover candidates is likely to flatten the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Event-driven hedge funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money call options on takeover candidates is likely to flatten the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.
cards.explanation: Out-of-the-money calls sit at high strikes, so extra demand for them lifts the right side of the curve and flattens rather than steepens the downward skew.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: An increase in the risk-free rate used to discount all option payoffs is likely to steepen the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.
cards.explanation: The risk-free rate enters BSM identically when pricing and when extracting implied volatility, so it has no systematic strike-dependent effect on the shape of the skew.
cards.originalText: An increase in the risk-free rate used to discount all option payoffs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: End users such as pension funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money put options for downside protection is likely to steepen the downward-sloping skew in equity index options.
cards.explanation: Out-of-the-money puts sit at low strikes, so extra demand for them raises low-strike implied volatility and steepens the downward skew. This is crashophobia expressed as order flow.
cards.originalText: End users such as pension funds increasing their demand for long positions in out-of-the-money put options for downside protection.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced.
cards.explanation: Exchange rates violate both lognormality conditions (constant volatility and no jumps). Both effects matter less at longer maturities, so the FX smile becomes less pronounced as maturity increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump; as option maturity increases, the volatility smile becomes more pronounced.
cards.explanation: The FX smile becomes less, not more, pronounced as time to maturity increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rates satisfy the constant volatility condition but violate the smooth-diffusion condition; the effect of jumps on implied volatility is independent of maturity.
cards.explanation: Exchange rate volatility is not constant, so both lognormality conditions fail. The impact of jumps on implied volatility is strongly maturity dependent and diminishes as maturity lengthens.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rate volatility is non-constant and exchange rates jump, but because both effects are strike-independent they shift the level of the curve without changing its shape.
cards.explanation: Non-constant volatility and jumps affect prices differently across strikes, which is exactly what creates the FX smile. A strike-independent effect would only shift the level of a flat curve.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an adequate representation of the price process of a currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
cards.explanation: A pegged currency is the archetypal jump process: it barely moves, then moves discontinuously when the peg is realigned or breaks. A pure diffusion such as GBM cannot generate that path.
cards.originalText: A currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
cards.correction: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an inadequate representation of the price process of a currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an inadequate representation of the price process of a currency held at a fixed peg to another currency by its central bank.
cards.explanation: A pegged currency is the archetypal jump process: it barely moves, then moves discontinuously when the peg is realigned or breaks. A pure diffusion such as GBM cannot generate that path.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Standard geometric Brownian motion is an adequate representation of the price process of any currency, provided the modelling horizon is short.
cards.explanation: Jumps matter most at short horizons because there is less diffusion to dilute them. The impact of jumps dissipates at long horizons, so a short horizon makes GBM less adequate, not more.
cards.originalText: Any currency, provided the modelling horizon is short.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: The downward-sloping volatility skew in equity index options is explained by capital structure leverage, whereby a fall in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and by crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money puts because they fear a repeat of a market crash.
cards.explanation: Falling equity value raises leverage and hence equity volatility (a negative price-volatility relationship), and crash fear bids up out-of-the-money puts. Both lift implied volatility at low strikes.
cards.originalText: Capital structure leverage, whereby a fall in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money puts because they fear a repeat of a market crash.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: The downward-sloping volatility skew in equity index options is explained by capital structure leverage, whereby a rise in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and by crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money calls because they fear missing a rally.
cards.explanation: Leverage rises when equity value falls, not when it rises, and crashophobia concerns out-of-the-money puts bought as crash insurance, not calls.
cards.originalText: Capital structure leverage, whereby a rise in equity value raises the debt-to-equity ratio and therefore raises equity volatility; and crashophobia, whereby traders bid up out-of-the-money calls because they fear missing a rally.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: A downward-sloping volatility term structure, with short-dated implied volatilities well above long-dated ones, is most plausibly explained by mean reversion in volatility.
cards.explanation: Mean-reverting volatility is pulled toward a long-run level, so when short-dated volatility is high it is expected to fall, producing a downward-sloping term structure.
cards.originalText: Mean reversion in volatility

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) includes a long-run variance term, which is always above the current conditional variance.
cards.explanation: The GARCH(1,1) long-run variance is a fixed parameter that can sit above or below the current conditional variance.
cards.originalText: Correct, because GARCH(1,1) includes a long-run variance term, which is always above the current conditional variance.
cards.correction: GARCH(1,1) includes a long-run variance term, which can be above or below the current conditional variance.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) includes a long-run variance term, which can be above or below the current conditional variance.
cards.explanation: The GARCH(1,1) long-run variance is a fixed parameter that can sit above or below the current conditional variance.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) implies mean reversion in volatility, so the volatility term structure slopes upward or downward depending on whether current volatility is below or above the long-run level.
cards.explanation: GARCH(1,1) has a fixed long-run variance with positive weight, so variance forecasts converge toward it. If current volatility is below the long-run level the term structure slopes upward; if above, it slopes downward.
cards.originalText: Incorrect, because GARCH(1,1) implies mean reversion in volatility, so the term structure slopes upward or downward depending on whether current volatility is below or above the long-run level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) implies no relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.
cards.explanation: Under GARCH(1,1), expected future variance depends strongly on current variance; the dependence decays as the horizon lengthens but does not vanish.
cards.originalText: Incorrect, because GARCH(1,1) implies no relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.
cards.correction: GARCH(1,1) implies a strong relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe volatility term structures and volatility surfaces and how they may be used to price options.
cards.statement: GARCH(1,1) implies a strong relationship between current volatility and expected future volatility.
cards.explanation: Under GARCH(1,1), expected future variance depends strongly on current variance; the dependence decays as the horizon lengthens but does not vanish.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.statement: When a stock is expected to jump sharply either up or down on an imminent announcement, the short-dated implied volatility curve is a pronounced smile, because the anticipated jump fattens both tails of the distribution relative to lognormal.
cards.explanation: A single anticipated two-sided jump makes the distribution bimodal, emptying the middle rather than extending the extremes. The result is a frown, not a smile.
cards.originalText: A pronounced smile, because the anticipated jump fattens both tails of the distribution relative to lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the impact of a single asset price jump on a volatility smile.
cards.statement: When a stock is expected to jump sharply either up or down on an imminent announcement, the short-dated implied volatility curve is a frown, because the anticipated jump makes the distribution bimodal, so at-the-money options are expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark while deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are cheap.
cards.explanation: A single anticipated two-sided jump concentrates probability at two points and hollows out the middle. At-the-money contracts become expensive and the wings cheap relative to lognormal, so the implied volatility curve frowns.
cards.originalText: A frown, because the anticipated jump makes the distribution bimodal, so at-the-money options are expensive relative to a lognormal benchmark while deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options are cheap.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the sum of two components, current VaR plus stressed VaR, whereas the FRTB requires only a single stressed expected shortfall.
cards.explanation: Basel II.5 summed current VaR and stressed VaR; the FRTB collapses this into a single expected shortfall calibrated to a 12-month stressed period.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated market risk capital using a single 10-day horizon, whereas the FRTB uses five different liquidity horizons depending on the liquidity of the market variable.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the fixed 10-day horizon with five liquidity horizons assigned according to the liquidity of each risk factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the default risk charge, which the FRTB eliminates, so that total market risk capital requirements are expected to fall.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge with a default risk charge rather than eliminating default risk capital, and total market risk capital is expected to rise rather than fall.
cards.correction: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the incremental risk charge, which the FRTB replaces, and total market risk capital requirements are expected to rise.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel II.5 required the incremental risk charge, which the FRTB replaces, and total market risk capital requirements are expected to rise.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge with a default risk charge rather than eliminating default risk capital, and total market risk capital is expected to rise rather than fall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The internal models approach under Basel I and II.5 calculated the requirement from VaR at a 99.0% confidence level, whereas the FRTB calculates it from expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.
cards.explanation: The FRTB moves the internal models measure from 99% VaR to 97.5% expected shortfall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The major motivation behind the FRTB's changes to the treatment of the trading book relative to the banking book is regulatory arbitrage between the two books.
cards.explanation: Pre-FRTB, the same economic exposure could attract a lower capital charge in one book than the other, so banks could choose their charge by choosing the book. The FRTB boundary rules aim to close that gap.
cards.originalText: Regulatory arbitrage between the two books

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 99% confidence level, which is materially more conservative for every distribution.
cards.explanation: The FRTB uses expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, not 99%, and it is not more conservative for every distribution; under normality it is almost equivalent to 99% VaR.
cards.correction: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which can be materially more conservative for a heavier-tailed distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which can be materially more conservative for a heavier-tailed distribution.
cards.explanation: The FRTB uses expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, not 99%, and it is not more conservative for every distribution; under normality it is almost equivalent to 99% VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level. For a normal distribution the two are almost exactly equivalent, but for a heavier-tailed distribution the 97.5% expected shortfall can be much greater than the 99% VaR.
cards.explanation: Under normality, 99% VaR is about 2.326 standard deviations and 97.5% ES about 2.338, so the switch is close to capital neutral. With heavier tails, the tail average can far exceed the quantile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces 99% VaR with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, which is necessarily lower than 99% VaR because the confidence level has been reduced.
cards.explanation: The lower confidence level is offset by moving from a quantile to a tail average; under normality 97.5% ES is almost exactly equal to 99% VaR, and with heavy tails it can be much larger.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains 99% VaR but requires it to be calculated over a stressed period rather than a current period.
cards.explanation: The FRTB does not retain VaR as the capital measure; it uses stressed expected shortfall at 97.5%. VaR survives only in backtesting.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under Basel II.5, stressed VaR is calibrated to a 250-day period of stressed market conditions.
cards.explanation: Stressed VaR under Basel II.5 is calculated from a 250-day (roughly one trading year) period of stressed market conditions; the FRTB carries this forward as a 12-month stressed period.
cards.originalText: A 250-day period

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A risk charge calculated under the sensitivities-based method is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach is the simple sum of the sensitivities-based method charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.
cards.originalText: A risk charge calculated under the sensitivities-based method

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A residual risk add-on is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The residual risk add-on is one of the three components and captures exotic underlyings and residual risks the other components do not reach.
cards.originalText: A residual risk add-on

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: A default risk charge is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The default risk charge is one of the three components and is the FRTB successor to the incremental risk charge.
cards.originalText: A default risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: An incremental risk charge is one of the three components of the FRTB standardised approach capital requirement.
cards.explanation: The incremental risk charge is the Basel II.5 measure that the FRTB replaced with the default risk charge. The three components are the sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.
cards.originalText: An incremental risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Credit spread risk, securitisation (correlation trading portfolio) is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Credit spread risk is split into three classes: non-securitisation, securitisation outside the correlation trading portfolio, and securitisation within it.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk, securitisation (correlation trading portfolio)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Funding liquidity risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Funding liquidity risk is governed by the LCR and NSFR, outside the market risk capital framework. The seven classes cover interest rate, three credit spread classes, equity, commodity and FX risk.
cards.originalText: Funding liquidity risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: General interest rate risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: General interest rate risk is the first of the seven sensitivities-based risk classes.
cards.originalText: General interest rate risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Commodity risk is one of the seven risk classes under the FRTB sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: Commodity risk is one of the seven sensitivities-based risk classes.
cards.originalText: Commodity risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for global systemically important banks with large and complex trading operations.
cards.explanation: Global systemically important banks with large trading operations are exactly the institutions for which the simplified approach is inadequate. It is intended for banks with low trading book activity or limited infrastructure.
cards.originalText: Global systemically important banks with large and complex trading operations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for banks whose trading desks have failed the backtesting exception thresholds.
cards.explanation: A desk that fails backtesting is moved to the full standardised approach as a sanction. The simplified standardised approach is a concession for small or unsophisticated banks, not a penalty.
cards.originalText: Banks whose trading desks have failed the backtesting exception thresholds.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The simplified standardised approach proposed by the Basel Committee in June 2017 is intended for banks with a low concentration of trading book activity, or that lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: The simplified standardised approach is a proportionality concession for small or unsophisticated banks, for which the full sensitivities-based method would be disproportionately costly.
cards.originalText: Banks with a low concentration of trading book activity, or that lack the infrastructure to implement the sensitivities-based method.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the standardised approach, the capital requirement is the sum of three components: a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge, and the residual risk add-on.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach requirement is the simple sum of the sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the internal models approach, the fixed 10-day liquidity horizon of Basel 2.5 is replaced by asset-class specific liquidity horizons of up to 120 days.
cards.explanation: The single 10-day horizon is replaced by five liquidity horizons running from 10 up to 120 days under the final standard.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the internal models approach, the 99.0% VaR of Basel 2.5, both current and stressed, is replaced by a 97.5% stressed expected shortfall.
cards.explanation: The headline change in the internal models risk measure is from 99% VaR (current plus stressed) to 97.5% stressed expected shortfall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under neither approach does the FRTB impose charges for credit-related exposures such as credit spread risk or jump-to-default risk, because those exposures are capitalised under the credit risk framework instead.
cards.explanation: The FRTB explicitly capitalises credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk within the market risk framework under both approaches, for example through the credit spread risk classes and the default risk charge.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital.
cards.explanation: Trading book positions are held with intent to trade, marked to market daily and attract market risk capital; banking book positions are expected to be held to maturity, are not marked to market daily and attract credit risk capital.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to credit risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and are subject to market risk capital.
cards.explanation: The capital regimes are the other way round: trading book instruments attract market risk capital and banking book instruments attract credit risk capital.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Instruments in both books are marked to market daily under the FRTB, but only trading book instruments attract market risk capital.
cards.explanation: The FRTB did not extend daily mark to market to the banking book; banking book instruments are carried at amortised or historical cost, which is why the boundary matters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Trading book instruments are valued at historical cost and are subject to market risk capital; banking book instruments are marked to market daily and are subject to liquidity risk capital.
cards.explanation: Trading book instruments are marked to market daily and attract market risk capital; banking book instruments are not marked to market daily and attract credit risk capital. There is no liquidity risk capital charge in this framework.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB collapses the banking book and the trading book into a single book, which removes the arbitrage opportunity entirely.
cards.explanation: The banking book and trading book remain distinct under the FRTB, attracting credit risk and market risk capital respectively. The FRTB instead makes the boundary more objective and limits movement between books.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB makes no change to the boundary but subjects both books to identical capital calculations.
cards.explanation: The FRTB substantially changes the boundary, making it more objective and restricting movement between books, and the two books are not subject to identical capital calculations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains a subjective intent-to-trade test as the necessary and sufficient condition for trading book inclusion, and imposes the incremental risk charge as a penalty when a position is moved between books.
cards.explanation: The FRTB moves away from a purely subjective intent-to-trade test toward objective criteria. The incremental risk charge was a Basel II.5 charge for credit-dependent trading book instruments, not a reclassification penalty.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary, including assignment at the point a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books.
cards.explanation: The FRTB closes the arbitrage by making the boundary objective (presumptive lists and evidence-based criteria), assigning positions at initiation, and strictly limiting subsequent reclassification.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, the backtesting methodology is unchanged from the earlier regime.
cards.explanation: FRTB backtesting changes from a single 99% one-day VaR test to tests at both 97.5% and 99%, applied at desk level with hard consequences.
cards.originalText: The backtesting methodology is unchanged under the FRTB.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data, is backtested at both the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at the level of each individual trading desk.
cards.explanation: The FRTB backtest uses one-day VaR on current (12-month) data, at both the 97.5% and 99% levels, applied to each trading desk, with hard consequences for breaches.
cards.originalText: A one-day static VaR, calibrated to the most recent 12 months of data, is backtested at BOTH the 97.5th and the 99th percentiles, at the level of each individual trading desk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, there are two backtests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall and a 10-day 99.0% stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: FRTB backtesting uses one-day VaR at 97.5% and 99%. Neither expected shortfall nor a stressed measure is backtested.
cards.originalText: There are two tests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall and a 10-day 99.0% stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, the backtesting horizon of 10 days and the 99.0% confidence level are unchanged, but they are now applied to expected shortfall rather than to VaR.
cards.explanation: The FRTB backtest horizon is one day, not 10, and the backtested measure is VaR, not expected shortfall.
cards.originalText: The 10-day horizon and the 99.0% confidence level are unchanged, but they are now applied to expected shortfall rather than to VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is not a coherent risk measure and so cannot be validated statistically.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure, which is one reason the FRTB adopted it. Coherence is unrelated to backtestability.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests one-day VaR on recent data rather than the expected shortfall used for capital because backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is difficult, and backtesting a stressed measure is in theory impossible, so a measure calibrated to current data is required.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall is a tail average with no threshold to breach, so it is hard to backtest, and a stressed measure calibrated to a historical stress window cannot be compared with current outcomes at all. The FRTB therefore backtests one-day VaR on current data.
cards.originalText: Backtesting a 10-day expected shortfall is difficult, and backtesting a STRESSED measure is in theory impossible, so a measure calibrated to current data is required.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Regulators require the backtest measure to match the measure used for the standardised approach, which is based on VaR.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardised approach is not based on VaR; it is the sum of a sensitivities-based charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on. Backtesting applies only to internal models.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, when a trading desk breaches the backtesting exception thresholds, all positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach, until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.
cards.explanation: A desk with more than 12 exceptions at the 99th percentile or more than 30 at the 97.5th in the most recent 12 months must capitalise all its positions under the standardised approach. The consequence is desk level and reversible once the desk is back within the thresholds.
cards.originalText: All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach, until the desk no longer exceeds the thresholds over the prior 12 months.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, when a trading desk breaches the backtesting exception thresholds, all positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach permanently, because internal models approval once withdrawn cannot be regained.
cards.explanation: The exclusion is not permanent: a desk returns to the internal models approach once it is back within both exception thresholds over the prior 12 months.
cards.originalText: All positions on the desk must be capitalised using the standardised approach permanently, because internal models approval once withdrawn cannot be regained.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB makes no change to the incremental risk charge.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.
cards.correction: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which recognises jump-to-default risk and mandates the inclusion of equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB separates credit spread risk (handled inside expected shortfall) from jump-to-default risk, and the default risk charge that replaces the IRC captures jump-to-default and extends to equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from downgrade risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly excludes equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, not downgrade risk (migration is captured within credit spread risk), and the default risk charge includes equity products rather than excluding them.
cards.correction: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly includes equity products.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, and replaces the IRC with the default risk charge, which explicitly includes equity products.
cards.explanation: The FRTB distinguishes credit spread risk from jump-to-default risk, not downgrade risk (migration is captured within credit spread risk), and the default risk charge includes equity products rather than excluding them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB retains the IRC but recalibrates it to a 10-day, 97.5% confidence expected shortfall, consistent with the market risk measure.
cards.explanation: The IRC is not retained; it is replaced by the default risk charge. Jump-to-default keeps a banking-book-style calibration of one year at 99.9%, not the 10-day 97.5% market risk parameters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach provided the bank's model has been approved for the correlation trading portfolio.
cards.explanation: Under the FRTB, all securitisation exposures, including the correlation trading portfolio, must be capitalised under the standardised approach; internal models are not available for them.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures may be capitalised under the internal models approach, but with a liquidity horizon floor of 120 days.
cards.explanation: There is no internal models route for securitisations under the FRTB; they must use the standardised approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures are exempt from market risk capital and attract credit risk capital in the banking book instead.
cards.explanation: Securitisation exposures held with trading intent remain in the trading book and attract market risk capital. The FRTB removes the choice of approach, requiring the standardised approach, not the applicability of the market risk framework.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Securitisation exposures must be capitalised under the STANDARDISED approach, because the internal models banks developed for these exposures under the earlier comprehensive risk measure differed widely from one another.
cards.explanation: Under the earlier comprehensive risk measure, banks' own models for securitisations differed widely, so similar exposures attracted very different capital. The FRTB therefore mandates the standardised approach for securitisations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Negative rates are attractive to lenders because they eliminate lending risk.
cards.explanation: A negative rate means the lender is repaid less than was lent, which makes lending unattractive. The rate paid is also unrelated to credit risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Negative short-term rates affect neither borrowers nor lenders, because rates revert to positive levels in the long run.
cards.explanation: Negative rates today affect borrowing and lending decisions today, regardless of where rates settle later, and a Gaussian model assigns positive probability to negative rates at every horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Negative rates cannot arise in practice because central banks are legally prohibited from setting a policy rate below zero.
cards.explanation: There is no legal prohibition on negative policy rates, and several major central banks have set them. The lower bound on rates is economic and approximate, not legal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Individuals will generally not lend at a negative rate, because they can instead hold cash and earn zero.
cards.explanation: Physical cash is a zero-yield alternative, so lending at a negative rate is dominated by holding cash. This creates the zero lower bound, which in practice sits slightly below zero because holding cash has storage and insurance costs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: When negative rates in an interest rate tree are set to zero, the rates in the original tree are the observed rates and the rates in the adjusted tree are the shadow rates.
cards.explanation: The labels are reversed: the original, unadjusted rates are the shadow rates, and the adjusted, floored rates are the observed rates.
cards.originalText: Original rates are the observed rates; adjusted rates are the shadow rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: When negative rates in an interest rate tree are set to zero, the rates in the original tree are the shadow rates and the rates in the adjusted tree are the observed rates.
cards.explanation: When a tree is built from the chosen distribution and negative nodes are set to zero, the unadjusted rates are shadow rates (hypothetical, possibly negative) and the floored rates are the observed, transactable rates used for discounting.
cards.originalText: Original rates are the shadow rates; adjusted rates are the observed rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Flooring a normally distributed tree at zero leaves the mean and volatility of the modelled rate unchanged, which is why it is preferred to changing the distribution.
cards.explanation: Truncating the left tail of a normally distributed tree at zero raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate. That distortion is the drawback of the flooring approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The only available method for preventing negative short-term rates in a term structure model is to adopt a distribution that cannot go negative, such as a lognormal or square-root process, because flooring a tree introduces arbitrage.
cards.explanation: Flooring a tree at zero is a recognised method alongside changing the distribution, and it does not introduce arbitrage; its cost is that it distorts the distribution.
cards.originalText: The only available method is to adopt a distribution that cannot go negative, such as a lognormal or square-root process, because flooring a tree introduces arbitrage.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: There are two methods for preventing negative short-term rates in a term structure model: flooring a normally distributed tree at zero, and adopting a distribution that cannot produce negative rates. Flooring raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate relative to the unadjusted model.
cards.explanation: Negative rates can be prevented either by flooring a tree at zero or by using a process that cannot go negative, such as lognormal or square-root. Truncating the left tail raises the mean and lowers the volatility.
cards.originalText: There are two methods: flooring a normally distributed tree at zero, and adopting a distribution that cannot produce negative rates. Flooring raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate relative to the unadjusted model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Methods for preventing negative short-term rates in term structure models are unnecessary in practice, since observed nominal short rates have never been negative.
cards.explanation: Negative nominal policy and market rates have been observed in Japan, Switzerland and the euro area, which is why preventing or handling negative rates matters in practice.
cards.originalText: There are two methods, but both are unnecessary in practice, since observed nominal short rates have never been negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model takes market prices as inputs, so it cannot judge whether they are fair. Assessing fair value calls for an equilibrium model.
cards.originalText: Determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.correction: The principal use of an equilibrium term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The principal use of an equilibrium term structure model is determining whether the market prices of actively traded securities are fair.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model takes market prices as inputs, so it cannot judge whether they are fair. Assessing fair value calls for an equilibrium model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is forecasting the level of the short-term rate over long horizons.
cards.explanation: The drift in an arbitrage-free model is a risk-neutral calibration parameter that bundles expectations with a risk premium, so it is not a real-world forecast of rates.
cards.originalText: Forecasting the level of the short-term rate over long horizons.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The principal use of an arbitrage-free term structure model is quoting the prices of securities that are not actively traded, on the basis of the prices of more liquid securities.
cards.explanation: An arbitrage-free model is calibrated to reproduce the prices of liquid securities exactly, so it is suited to pricing illiquid securities consistently with the liquid instruments used to hedge them.
cards.originalText: Quoting the prices of securities that are not actively traded, on the basis of the prices of more liquid securities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An exact fit of an arbitrage-free term structure model to market prices guarantees that the model will continue to price accurately as the term structure moves, because the calibration is re-derived at every node.
cards.explanation: Fitting today's prices says nothing about tomorrow's. Arbitrage-free models generally need recalibration as the curve moves, and frequent large refits indicate instability.
cards.originalText: An exact fit guarantees that the model will continue to price accurately as the term structure moves, because the calibration is re-derived at every node.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
