cards.explanation: Extreme value theory uses only tail observations and deliberately ignores the body of the distribution.
cards.originalText: EVT makes use of all information in the entire distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Applying the generalized extreme value distribution to block maxima requires the parent distribution $F(x)$ to be specified.
cards.explanation: Like the central limit theorem, the Fisher-Tippett result does not require the parent distribution to be known. The GEV is the limit law whatever the parent.
cards.originalText: Only I, because F(x) must be specified.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Applying the generalized extreme value distribution to block maxima requires the parent distribution to be normal.
cards.explanation: The GEV applies for any parent distribution. A Student's t parent simply implies a heavy tail, the Frechet case with $\xi > 0$.
cards.originalText: Only II, because the parent must be normal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: The regression method orders the extreme observations and obtains least squares estimates of the extreme value parameters.
cards.explanation: Regression estimation ranks the extreme values and fits the parameters by least squares, which is easier than maximum likelihood.
cards.originalText: The regression method orders the extreme observations and obtains least squares estimates of the EV parameters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: The maximum likelihood method estimates the tail index by averaging a chosen number of the most extreme observations.
cards.explanation: Averaging the most extreme observations describes the semi-parametric Hill estimator. Maximum likelihood maximises a likelihood function.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: The Hill estimator is insensitive to how many tail observations are included.
cards.explanation: The Hill estimator is highly sensitive to the number of tail observations included, and choosing that number is its main challenge.
cards.correction: The Hill estimator is highly sensitive to how many tail observations are included.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Maximum likelihood is simple to apply because it needs no optimization of a likelihood function.
cards.explanation: Maximum likelihood requires maximising a complex likelihood function, so it is harder, not simpler, than regression.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the distribution of excess losses over a threshold $u$ is defined as $P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\}$.
cards.explanation: POT conditions on the threshold being exceeded, $X > u$, and models the excess $X - u$ rather than the loss itself.
cards.originalText: $P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\}$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the distribution of excess losses over a threshold $u$ is defined as $P\{X \le x \mid X > u\}$.
cards.explanation: This conditions correctly on $X > u$ but models the loss $X$ rather than the excess $X - u$.
cards.originalText: $P\{X \le x \mid X > u\}$
cards.correction: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the distribution of excess losses over a threshold $u$ is defined as $P\{X - u \le x \mid X > u\}$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, if the number of observations rises with no additional exceedances of the threshold, the exceedance frequency falls and the VaR and ES estimates decrease.
cards.explanation: A smaller $N_u/N$ places the target tail probability closer to the threshold, so the estimated VaR and ES fall.
cards.originalText: Increase N from 1,350 to 1,500 with no additional exceedances, so N(u)/N falls

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, both VaR and expected shortfall can be computed from the estimated generalized Pareto scale and tail index (with $\xi < 1$), the threshold and the exceedance count.
cards.explanation: POT gives a fully specified parametric tail beyond the threshold, so VaR and ES both have closed-form expressions, with ES finite when $\xi < 1$.
cards.originalText: Both VaR and expected shortfall can be computed from these estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, only VaR can be computed from the fitted generalized Pareto parameters; expected shortfall needs a separate non-parametric estimate.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall has a closed-form expression from the same parameters, finite when $\xi < 1$.
cards.originalText: Only VaR can be computed; expected shortfall needs a separate non‑parametric estimate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, only expected shortfall can be computed from the fitted generalized Pareto parameters; VaR needs a separate non-parametric estimate.
cards.explanation: VaR has the standard POT formula $u + \frac{\beta}{\xi}\left[\left(\frac{n}{N_u}(1-\alpha)\right)^{-\xi} - 1\right]$, and ES follows from it.
cards.originalText: Only expected shortfall can be computed; VaR needs a separate non‑parametric estimate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable but increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: The generalized Pareto approximation is only valid as the threshold becomes large, so a low threshold weakens it, but more observations exceed the threshold, which gives more data for estimating the parameters.
cards.originalText: less applicable but increases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable but decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: A low threshold moves away from the region where the generalized Pareto approximation is valid and puts more observations above the threshold.
cards.originalText: more applicable but decreases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.
cards.correction: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable but increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable and decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: A lower threshold increases the number of exceedances, trading generalized Pareto validity for sample size.
cards.originalText: less applicable and decreases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.
cards.correction: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable and increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable and increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: A low threshold weakens the generalized Pareto approximation, so the model is less applicable even though more observations are used.
cards.originalText: more applicable but increases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.
cards.correction: Setting the threshold relatively low in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable and increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively high in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable, but decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: A higher threshold improves the generalized Pareto approximation, so the model is more applicable, but fewer losses exceed it. The threshold must therefore balance approximation quality against sample size.
cards.originalText: more applicable, but decreases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively high in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable, but increases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: Raising the threshold reduces the number of exceedances, so fewer observations are available for estimation. The benefit of a high threshold is a better generalized Pareto fit.
cards.originalText: more applicable, but increases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.
cards.correction: Setting the threshold relatively high in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable, but decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Setting the threshold relatively high in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model less applicable, and decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.
cards.explanation: A high threshold improves, rather than harms, the generalized Pareto approximation. It does reduce the number of exceedances available for estimation.
cards.originalText: less applicable, and decreases the number of observations in the modeling procedure.
cards.correction: Setting the threshold relatively high in the peaks-over-threshold approach makes the model more applicable, and decreases the number of observations used in the modeling procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Raising the threshold in the peaks-over-threshold approach offers the benefit of lower bias but the drawback of higher variance.
cards.explanation: POT involves a bias-variance trade-off. A higher threshold improves the generalized Pareto approximation (lower bias) but leaves fewer exceedances, which raises the variance of the estimates.
cards.originalText: The higher threshold offers the benefit of lower bias but the drawback of higher variance.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Raising the threshold in the peaks-over-threshold approach offers the benefit of lower variance but the drawback of higher bias.
cards.explanation: The direction is reversed. A higher threshold leaves fewer exceedances, which raises variance, while it improves the generalized Pareto fit, which lowers bias.
cards.originalText: The higher threshold offers the benefit of lower variance but the drawback of higher bias.
cards.correction: Raising the threshold in the peaks-over-threshold approach offers the benefit of lower bias but the drawback of higher variance.

changes.from: lower variance but the drawback of higher bias
changes.to: lower bias but the drawback of higher variance

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: A peaks-over-threshold analyst can avoid a subjective choice of the threshold by applying an analytical maximum log-likelihood function to all three parameters simultaneously.
cards.explanation: Maximum likelihood estimates the scale and shape parameters only after a threshold has been chosen. The threshold itself remains a judgmental choice, usually guided by mean excess and parameter stability plots.
cards.originalText: He can avoid a subjective choice of the threshold by applying an analytical maximum log‑likelihood function to all three parameters simultaneously.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires fewer estimated parameters than the GEV approach and shares one parameter with it.
cards.explanation: GEV needs an extra location parameter, whereas POT replaces it with a chosen threshold. Both approaches share the tail index $\xi$.
cards.originalText: fewer estimated parameters than GEV and shares one parameter with GEV

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires more estimated parameters than the GEV approach and shares one parameter with it.
cards.explanation: POT needs fewer parameters because GEV carries the additional location parameter. The shared parameter is the tail index $\xi$.
cards.originalText: more estimated parameters than GEV and shares one parameter with GEV
cards.correction: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires fewer estimated parameters than the GEV approach and shares one parameter with it.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires fewer estimated parameters than the GEV approach and does not share any parameters with it.
cards.explanation: The two approaches share the tail index $\xi$. POT does need fewer estimated parameters because the threshold replaces GEV's location parameter.
cards.originalText: fewer estimated parameters than the GEV approach and does not share any parameters with the GEV approach.
cards.correction: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires fewer estimated parameters than the GEV approach and shares one parameter with it.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach makes more efficient use of the available data than the GEV block-maxima approach.
cards.explanation: POT fits a generalized Pareto distribution to all exceedances over a high threshold. Block maxima keep only one observation per block and discard other potentially valuable extreme observations.
cards.originalText: Makes more efficient use of the available data

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach does not require any parameter estimation.
cards.explanation: POT still requires estimating the scale and shape (tail index) parameters of the generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.originalText: Does not require any parameter estimation

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach is based on the distribution of a single maximum per block.
cards.explanation: Using one maximum per block describes the GEV block-maxima approach, which is the source of its data loss. POT models all exceedances over a high threshold.
cards.originalText: Is based on the distribution of a single maximum per block

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Neither the GEV approach nor the POT approach is superior in all circumstances; each has advantages, and the choice depends on the data and the trade-offs involved.
cards.explanation: GEV avoids choosing a threshold but wastes data, whereas POT uses data more efficiently but must deal with threshold-choice uncertainty. Neither dominates in every case.
cards.originalText: Neither approach is superior in all circumstances; each has advantages and the choice depends on the data and the trade‑offs involved.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The GEV approach is superior to the POT approach in virtually all circumstances because it avoids choosing a threshold.
cards.explanation: GEV avoids a threshold but wastes data and needs an extra location parameter. Neither approach is superior in all circumstances.
cards.originalText: GEV is superior in virtually all circumstances because it avoids choosing a threshold.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The POT approach is superior to the GEV approach in virtually all circumstances because it always uses more data.
cards.explanation: POT's data efficiency is offset by uncertainty over the threshold choice, so it is not universally superior. The better approach depends on the data and the trade-offs involved.
cards.originalText: POT is superior in virtually all circumstances because it always uses more data.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The GEV and POT approaches are unrelated methods and cannot be compared.
cards.explanation: Both approaches stem from extreme value theory, share the tail index $\xi$ and can be compared on data use, parameter count and tuning choices.
cards.originalText: They are unrelated methods and cannot be compared.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach to extreme value theory are parametric.
cards.explanation: Both impose a parametric distribution on the extremes: the generalized extreme value distribution for block maxima and the generalized Pareto distribution for exceedances.
cards.originalText: Both GEV and POT

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Neither the GEV approach nor the POT approach to extreme value theory is parametric.
cards.explanation: Both fit parametric distributions to extremes, unlike non-parametric methods such as historical simulation.
cards.originalText: Neither GEV nor POT
cards.correction: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach to extreme value theory are parametric.

changes.from: Neither the GEV approach nor the POT approach
changes.to: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The GEV block-maxima approach is more likely than the POT approach to imply a loss of potentially useful data.
cards.explanation: Block maxima keep only the largest observation in each block and discard other extreme observations, whereas POT uses every exceedance over the threshold.
cards.originalText: GEV (block maxima)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The POT approach is more likely than the GEV block-maxima approach to imply a loss of potentially useful data.
cards.explanation: POT uses every exceedance over the threshold, so its main issue is threshold choice. Block maxima discard all but one observation per block.
cards.originalText: Peaks‑over‑threshold (POT)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The POT approach has the disadvantage of requiring the analyst to choose a threshold.
cards.explanation: Only POT depends on a threshold, and that choice is inevitably judgmental and adds uncertainty through a bias-variance trade-off.
cards.originalText: Peaks‑over‑threshold (POT)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The GEV block-maxima approach has the disadvantage of requiring the analyst to choose a threshold.
cards.explanation: GEV has no threshold; its tuning choice is the block length. The threshold choice is the drawback of POT.
cards.originalText: GEV (block maxima)
cards.correction: The GEV block-maxima approach has the disadvantage of requiring the analyst to choose a block length.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach can model a light or a heavy tail, depending on the value of the tail (shape) index $\xi$.
cards.explanation: Both approaches share the tail index $\xi$, and its value determines how heavy the tail is.
cards.originalText: Both GEV and POT

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Neither the GEV approach nor the POT approach can model a light or a heavy tail through the value of the tail (shape) index $\xi$.
cards.explanation: Both approaches use the tail index $\xi$, and its value determines the tail heaviness.
cards.originalText: Neither GEV nor POT
cards.correction: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach can model a light or a heavy tail through the value of the tail (shape) index $\xi$.

changes.from: Neither the GEV approach nor the POT approach can
changes.to: Both the GEV approach and the POT approach can

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Both the GEV and POT approaches automatically and easily fit distributions to a stochastic process with autocorrelated clusters.
cards.explanation: Both approaches rest on an i.i.d. assumption, so autocorrelated clusters are not fitted automatically or easily.
cards.originalText: Each of the approaches automatically and easily fits distributions to a stochastic process with autocorrelated clusters

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: In both the GEV and POT approaches, the fitted parametric distribution has a parameter, the tail index $\xi$, that can be increased to model increasingly heavier tails.
cards.explanation: The tail index $\xi$ appears in both the GEV and the generalized Pareto distribution, and a higher value gives a heavier tail.
cards.originalText: Each of the fitted EV parametric distributions has a parameter that can be increased to model increasingly heavier tails

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Under extreme value theory, a parametric distribution of extreme values can be fitted to actual datasets without knowledge of the underlying parent distribution.
cards.explanation: The extreme value theorems are distribution-free with respect to the parent distribution, which is why EVT can be applied without knowing it.
cards.originalText: She can fit a parametric distribution of extreme values to actual datasets without knowledge of the underlying distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Unlike basic historical simulation, EVT-based VaR or ES can return values that exceed the greatest loss in the actual historical dataset.
cards.explanation: Parametric extrapolation of the tail allows estimates beyond the largest observed loss, whereas basic historical simulation is capped by the sample maximum.
cards.originalText: Unlike basic historical simulation, the EVT VaR or ES can return value(s) that exceed the greatest loss in the actual historical dataset

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Block maxima is superior to POT because it uses the data more efficiently, and its Gumbel instance avoids the trade-off between bias and variance.
cards.explanation: Block maxima discard all but the largest loss in each block, so they use data less efficiently than POT. Choosing the block length also involves an unavoidable bias-variance trade-off.
cards.originalText: Block maxima is superior to POT because it uses the data more efficiently, and its Gumbel instance avoids the trade‑off between bias and variance

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: If the parent distribution is a Levy distribution, the extremes fall in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution.
cards.explanation: Heavy-tailed parent distributions such as the Levy, Student t or Pareto have extremes in the Frechet domain of attraction.
cards.originalText: If the parent distribution is a Levy distribution, the extremes fall in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: For a given historical window, shorter blocks (and therefore more blocks) achieve lower variance but with more bias.
cards.explanation: Shorter blocks give more block maxima, which lowers the variance of the estimates, but the maxima are then less likely to be true extremes, which adds bias.
cards.originalText: For a given historical window, shorter blocks (and therefore more blocks) achieve lower variance but with more bias

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: Time dependency in loss data can be addressed with longer (and therefore fewer) blocks, giving less bias but at the cost of higher variance.
cards.explanation: Longer blocks reduce the bias caused by time dependency but leave fewer block maxima, which increases the variance of the estimates.
cards.originalText: Time dependency in the loss data can be addressed with longer (and therefore fewer) blocks, giving less bias but at the cost of higher variance

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: An advantage of the POT approach is that the distribution of extreme losses over a high threshold is assumed to always have the same form regardless of the distribution of all losses.
cards.explanation: The Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem gives a generalized Pareto form for exceedances over a high threshold, independent of the parent distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The block maxima approach avoids the data loss issues that sometimes arise under the POT approach, which constitutes an advantage of GEV compared to POT.
cards.explanation: It is block maxima that tends to lose data, since only one observation per block is kept. Data loss is a disadvantage of GEV, not of POT.
cards.originalText: The block maxima approach can avoid the data loss issues that sometimes arise under the POT approach, which constitutes an advantage of GEV compared to POT.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: The additional parameter in the POT approach that is not in the GEV approach is a location parameter measuring the central tendency of the extreme loss distribution.
cards.explanation: The location parameter is the extra parameter in GEV, not POT. POT has fewer parameters because it uses a chosen threshold instead.
cards.originalText: The additional parameter that is included in the POT approach, but not the GEV approach, is a location parameter that measures the central tendency of the extreme loss distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the generalized extreme value (GEV) and POT approaches to estimating extreme risks.
cards.statement: A drawback of the GEV approach is that the parameter estimates suffer from the subjective choice of the threshold above which losses are considered extreme.
cards.explanation: The threshold is chosen in POT, not in GEV. GEV's tuning choice is the block length.
cards.originalText: A drawback of the GEV approach is that the parameter estimates describing the extreme loss distribution suffer from the fact that the choice of the threshold over which losses are considered extreme is subjective.
cards.correction: A drawback of the POT approach is that the parameter estimates suffer from the subjective choice of the threshold above which losses are considered extreme.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: As the threshold is increased, the distribution of losses exceeding it converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.explanation: The Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem says that excess losses over a sufficiently high threshold follow a generalized Pareto distribution, irrespective of the parent distribution.
cards.originalText: As the threshold value is increased, the distribution of losses over a fixed threshold value converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: If the tail parameter of the generalized extreme value distribution goes to infinity, the GEV essentially becomes a normal distribution.
cards.explanation: A tail index of zero, not infinity, gives the light-tailed Gumbel case, whose tails resemble those of normal or lognormal distributions.
cards.originalText: If the tail parameter value of the generalized extreme‑value (GEV) distribution goes to infinity, then the GEV essentially becomes a normal distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: To apply extreme value theory, the underlying loss distribution must be either normal or lognormal.
cards.explanation: EVT is valuable precisely because it models tails without assuming a particular parent distribution. Normal and lognormal parents are merely examples of the $\xi = 0$ case.
cards.originalText: To apply EVT, the underlying loss distribution must be either normal or lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: The number of exceedances decreases as the threshold value decreases, which causes the reliability of the parameter estimates to increase.
cards.explanation: Lowering the threshold increases the number of exceedances, which lowers the variance of the estimates but worsens the generalized Pareto approximation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: As the threshold $u$ gets large, the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem states that the distribution of above-threshold observations converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.explanation: This theorem is the POT counterpart of the Fisher-Tippett theorem: excesses over a high threshold follow a generalized Pareto distribution whatever the parent distribution.
cards.originalText: a generalized Pareto distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: As the threshold $u$ gets large, the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem states that the distribution of above-threshold observations converges to a generalized extreme value distribution.
cards.explanation: The GEV describes block maxima (Fisher-Tippett), whereas threshold exceedances converge to a generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.originalText: a generalized extreme value distribution
cards.correction: As the threshold $u$ gets large, the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem states that the distribution of above-threshold observations converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: As the threshold $u$ gets large, the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem states that the distribution of above-threshold observations converges to a normal distribution.
cards.explanation: Exceedances over a high threshold converge to a generalized Pareto distribution, not a normal distribution.
cards.originalText: a normal distribution
cards.correction: As the threshold $u$ gets large, the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem states that the distribution of above-threshold observations converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: The generalized Pareto distribution used in the POT approach needs scale and tail (shape) index parameters, and in addition the threshold $u$ must be specified.
cards.explanation: The excess losses need $\beta$ and $\xi$, while the threshold $u$ is a user-chosen input that takes the place of GEV's location parameter.
cards.originalText: Scale and tail/shape index parameters, plus the threshold (u) must be specified

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: The generalized Pareto distribution used in the POT approach needs scale, location and tail (shape) index parameters, plus a specified threshold $u$.
cards.explanation: The location parameter belongs to the GEV (block maxima) distribution. The POT distribution needs only scale and tail index, plus the threshold.
cards.originalText: Scale, location, and tail/shape index parameters, plus the threshold (u) must be specified
cards.correction: The generalized Pareto distribution used in the POT approach needs scale and tail (shape) index parameters, plus a specified threshold $u$.

changes.from: scale, location and tail (shape) index parameters

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Choosing a higher threshold in the POT approach gives better convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution but fewer data points on which to make estimates.
cards.explanation: The threshold must be high enough for the generalized Pareto approximation to hold but low enough to retain enough exceedances for reliable estimation.
cards.originalText: Better convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution but fewer data points on which to make estimates

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Choosing a higher threshold in the POT approach gives more data points but less convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.explanation: Both effects are reversed: a higher threshold gives fewer data points and better convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution.
cards.originalText: More data points but less convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution
cards.correction: Choosing a higher threshold in the POT approach gives fewer data points but better convergence to the generalized Pareto distribution.

changes.from: more data points but less convergence
changes.to: fewer data points but better convergence

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Raising the threshold in the POT approach for the same dataset decreases the proportion of observations that exceed it, $N(u)/N$.
cards.explanation: Fewer losses exceed a higher threshold, so the exceedance proportion $N(u)/N$ falls mechanically.
cards.originalText: If she increases the threshold for the same dataset, she should expect N(u)/N to decrease but with unclear effect on VaR and ES (they may increase or decrease)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Increasing the threshold in the POT approach increases the bias of the estimates.
cards.explanation: A higher threshold reduces bias because the generalized Pareto approximation is better. The cost is fewer exceedances and so higher variance.
cards.originalText: If she increases the threshold, the bias increases
cards.correction: Increasing the threshold in the POT approach decreases the bias of the estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Increasing the threshold in the POT approach decreases the variance of the estimates.
cards.explanation: A higher threshold leaves fewer exceedances, which increases the variance of the estimates.
cards.originalText: If she increases the threshold, the variance decreases
cards.correction: Increasing the threshold in the POT approach increases the variance of the estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: Maximum likelihood estimation can be used to determine the objectively optimal threshold in the POT approach.
cards.explanation: Maximum likelihood fits the scale and shape parameters given a threshold. The threshold choice itself stays subjective and judgmental.
cards.originalText: She should employ maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to determine the objectively optimal threshold

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Buying an option on the better of two assets, with payoff $\max(S_1, S_2)$, gains value if correlation between the assets falls.
cards.explanation: Lower correlation increases dispersion between the assets, which raises the expected maximum. A long position in the better-of option is therefore short correlation.
cards.originalText: Buy an option on the better of two assets, payoff = max$(S_{1}, S_{2})$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Buying an option on the worse of two assets, with payoff $\min(S_1, S_2)$, gains value if correlation between the assets falls.
cards.explanation: The worse-of option is long correlation: its price falls as correlation falls because dispersion makes it more likely that one asset lags badly.
cards.originalText: Buy an option on the worse of two assets, payoff = min$(S_{1}, S_{2})$.
cards.correction: Buying an option on the worse of two assets, with payoff $\min(S_1, S_2)$, gains value if correlation between the assets rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Buying correlation in a correlation swap (paying the fixed rate and receiving realized correlation) gains value if correlation falls.
cards.explanation: The buyer of a correlation swap pays fixed and receives realized correlation, so the position profits when correlation rises.
cards.originalText: Buy correlation in a correlation swap (pay the fixed rate, receive realized correlation).
cards.correction: Buying correlation in a correlation swap (paying the fixed rate and receiving realized correlation) gains value if correlation rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Selling an exchange option, with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$, gains value if correlation between the assets falls.
cards.explanation: An exchange option's price rises as correlation falls, so a short position loses; the seller is long correlation.
cards.originalText: Sell (short) an exchange option, payoff = max$(0, S_{2} - S_{1})$.
cards.correction: Selling an exchange option, with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$, gains value if correlation between the assets rises.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A negative correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency's value in the domestic currency increases the price of a quanto call on that index.
cards.explanation: When the index is high the foreign currency tends to be weaker, so the seller needs more foreign currency to deliver the fixed-rate conversion of the profit. A quanto call's price therefore rises as correlation falls.
cards.originalText: Negative correlation increases the price, because the euro tends to weaken as the DAX rises, so the seller needs more euros to convert the profit into dollars.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A positive correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency's value in the domestic currency increases the price of a quanto call on that index.
cards.explanation: Positive correlation lowers the price of a quanto call, because the foreign currency tends to strengthen along with the index.
cards.originalText: Positive correlation increases the price, because the euro strengthens as the DAX rises and the seller needs more euros to cover the payoff.
cards.correction: A positive correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency's value in the domestic currency decreases the price of a quanto call on that index.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A negative correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency's value in the domestic currency decreases the price of a quanto call on that index.
cards.explanation: Negative correlation raises the price of a quanto call. Correlation does not change whether the call finishes in the money; it changes the cost to the seller of converting the payoff at the fixed rate.
cards.originalText: Negative correlation decreases the price, because the euro strengthens as the DAX falls and the call becomes less likely to finish in the money.
cards.correction: A negative correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency's value in the domestic currency increases the price of a quanto call on that index.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Correlation between a foreign equity index and the foreign currency has no effect on the price of a quanto call, because the conversion rate is fixed at inception.
cards.explanation: The fixed rate only removes the buyer's currency risk. The seller still bears it, so correlation is a pricing input.
cards.originalText: Correlation has no effect on the price, because the conversion rate is fixed at inception.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets increases the price of an option on the worse of the two assets.
cards.explanation: High correlation keeps the poorer asset from lagging far behind the other, which raises the worse-of option's value. It is the exception among multi-asset options, most of which fall in price as correlation rises.
cards.originalText: Option on the worse of two: payoff = min$(S_{1}, S_{2})$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets increases the price of a call on the maximum of the two assets.
cards.explanation: The call on the maximum gains from dispersion, so its price falls as correlation rises.
cards.originalText: Call on the maximum of two: payoff = max$[0, \text{max}(S_{1}, S_{2}) - K]$
cards.correction: An increase in the correlation between two assets decreases the price of a call on the maximum of the two assets.

cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets increases the price of an exchange option with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$.
cards.explanation: The spread between the assets barely moves as correlation approaches 1, so the exchange option price approaches zero and falls with correlation.
cards.originalText: Exchange option: payoff = max$(0, S_{2} - S_{1})$
cards.correction: An increase in the correlation between two assets decreases the price of an exchange option with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An increase in the correlation between two assets increases the price of a spread call option with payoff $\max[0, (S_2 - S_1) - K]$.
cards.explanation: The spread call depends on the volatility of $S_2 - S_1$, which shrinks as correlation rises, so its price falls.
cards.originalText: Spread call option: payoff = max$[0, (S_{2} - S_{1}) - K]$
cards.correction: An increase in the correlation between two assets decreases the price of a spread call option with payoff $\max[0, (S_2 - S_1) - K]$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For a rainbow option on assets $S$, $Q$ and $C$ with strike $K$, the expression $\max[0, \max(S, Q, C) - K]$ is a valid call payoff.
cards.explanation: This is a rainbow call on the maximum of the three assets, floored at zero.
cards.originalText: Call: max$[0, \text{max}(S, Q, C) - K]$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For a rainbow option on assets $S$, $Q$ and $C$ with strike $K$, the expression $\max(S, Q, C, K) - K$ is a valid call payoff.
cards.explanation: Taking the maximum with $K$ and subtracting $K$ floors the payoff at zero, so it equals $\max[0, \max(S, Q, C) - K]$.
cards.originalText: Call: max$[S, Q, C, K] - K$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For a rainbow option on assets $S$, $Q$ and $C$ with strike $K$, the expression $\max[0, K - \min(S, Q, C)]$ is a valid put payoff.
cards.explanation: This is a rainbow put on the minimum of the three assets, floored at zero.
cards.originalText: Put: max$[0, K - \text{min}(S, Q, C)]$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An exchange option, with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$, is one type of multi-asset (rainbow) option whose payoff depends on the difference of two assets.
cards.explanation: Exchange options belong to the broader class of multi-asset options because their payoff depends on two underlying assets, $S_1$ and $S_2$.
cards.originalText: An exchange option is one type of multi‑asset (rainbow) option, whose payoff max$(0, S_{2} - S_{1})$ depends on the difference of two assets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A rainbow option is a special case of an exchange option.
cards.explanation: The relationship runs the other way: the exchange option is one member of the broader class of multi-asset options.
cards.correction: An exchange option is a special case of a rainbow option.

changes.from: A rainbow option is a special case of an exchange option
changes.to: An exchange option is a special case of a rainbow option

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Exchange options are single-asset options, so they are unrelated to rainbow options.
cards.explanation: An exchange option depends on two assets, $S_1$ and $S_2$, so it is a multi-asset option.
cards.originalText: Exchange options are single‑asset options, so they are unrelated to rainbow options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: As the correlation between two assets falls, the price of a call option on the worse of the two assets decreases.
cards.explanation: Lower correlation makes it more likely that one asset underperforms, which reduces the payoff based on the minimum. Most other multi-asset options gain from the greater dispersion.
cards.originalText: A call option on the worse of two assets (payoff based on min$(S_{1}, S_{2})$)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: As the correlation between two assets falls, the price of an exchange option with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$ decreases.
cards.explanation: The exchange option's price rises as correlation falls because the volatility of the spread increases; near perfect correlation its value is close to zero.
cards.originalText: An exchange option with payoff max$(0, S_{2} - S_{1})$
cards.correction: As the correlation between two assets falls, the price of an exchange option with payoff $\max(0, S_2 - S_1)$ increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: As the correlation between two assets falls, the price of a call option on the better of the two assets decreases.
cards.explanation: The better-of option benefits from dispersion, so its price rises when correlation falls.
cards.originalText: A call option on the better of two assets
cards.correction: As the correlation between two assets falls, the price of a call option on the better of the two assets increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: As the correlation between the underlying foreign index and the exchange rate falls, the price of a quanto call decreases.
cards.explanation: Lower correlation raises quanto prices, so reversing this sign is a common error.
cards.originalText: A quanto call on a foreign equity index
cards.correction: As the correlation between the underlying foreign index and the exchange rate falls, the price of a quanto call increases.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Both rainbow options and basket options have payoffs that depend on two or more underlying assets.
cards.explanation: Both are multi-asset exotic options, which is why correlation between the underlyings is a pricing input.
cards.originalText: Both have payoffs that depend on two or more underlying assets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A basket option depends on one asset only, through the average of its prices over time.
cards.explanation: Averaging one asset's prices over time describes an Asian option. A basket option is an option on a portfolio of several assets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A rainbow option depends on a single asset but has several possible strike prices.
cards.explanation: A rainbow option is defined by multiple underlying assets, not by multiple strikes.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Only rainbow options depend on multiple assets; a basket option is a single-asset option with several exercise dates.
cards.explanation: A basket option is an option on a portfolio of several assets, so it is also a multi-asset option.
cards.originalText: Only rainbow options depend on multiple assets; a basket option is a single‑asset option with several exercise dates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Lower correlation raises the price of most multi-asset options, such as an exchange option, but it lowers the price of a call on the worse of two assets.
cards.explanation: Lower correlation widens the dispersion between assets and raises the price of most multi-asset options. The worse-of option is the exception.
cards.originalText: Lower correlation raises the price of most multi‑asset options (such as an exchange option), but it lowers the price of a call on the worse of two assets.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: An exchange option is worth the most when the two asset prices are almost perfectly positively correlated.
cards.explanation: As correlation approaches 1, the spread $S_2 - S_1$ barely changes and the exchange option's price approaches zero.
cards.correction: An exchange option is worth the least when the two asset prices are almost perfectly positively correlated.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Correlation affects the price of rainbow options but is irrelevant to basket options.
cards.explanation: A basket's value depends on portfolio variance, which depends on the pairwise correlations, so correlation matters for baskets too.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A higher correlation increases the price of every multi-asset correlation option.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation generally lowers the price of multi-asset options such as exchange and best-of options; the worse-of option is an exception in the other direction.
cards.originalText: A higher correlation increases the price of every multi‑asset correlation option.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A call option whose payoff is based on the higher of two stock prices at maturity (a best-of option) is an example of a rainbow option.
cards.explanation: Best-of and worst-of options are classic rainbow options because their payoff depends on the maximum or minimum of multiple assets.
cards.originalText: A call option whose payoff is based on the higher of two stock prices at maturity (best‑of option).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A call on a single stock whose payoff is based on the average of that stock's daily closing prices is an example of a rainbow option.
cards.explanation: This is an Asian option, which is path-dependent on a single asset, not a multi-asset option.
cards.originalText: A call on a single stock whose payoff is based on the average of that stock’s daily closing prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A plain-vanilla put on a single stock is an example of a rainbow option.
cards.explanation: A vanilla option has a single underlying asset, whereas a rainbow option depends on several.
cards.originalText: A plain‑vanilla put on a single stock.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A call on a single stock that is knocked out if the price touches a barrier is an example of a rainbow option.
cards.explanation: A barrier option is path-dependent on one asset, and no second asset is involved.
cards.originalText: A call on a single stock that is knocked out if the price touches a barrier.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The average of two lognormally distributed asset prices is in general not lognormal, so a basket option has no simple closed-form lognormal pricing formula and is priced with approximations or Monte Carlo simulation.
cards.explanation: Sums of the log prices stay normal, but sums of the prices themselves do not stay lognormal. Basket options are therefore typically valued by approximation or simulation.
cards.originalText: In general the average price is not lognormal, so there is no simple closed‑form lognormal pricing formula and approximations or Monte Carlo simulation are used.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The average of two lognormally distributed asset prices is lognormal, with volatility equal to the average of the two volatilities.
cards.explanation: Lognormality is not preserved under addition, and the volatilities do not simply average.
cards.originalText: The average price is lognormal, with volatility equal to the average of the two volatilities.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The average of two lognormally distributed asset prices is normally distributed, because the sum of normal variables is normal.
cards.explanation: The sum-of-normals result applies to log prices, not to prices. The prices are lognormal, and their average is in general neither normal nor lognormal.
cards.originalText: The average price is normally distributed, because the sum of normal variables is normal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The average of two lognormally distributed asset prices is lognormal only when the correlation between the prices is zero.
cards.explanation: Zero correlation does not make a sum of lognormal variables lognormal; the average is not lognormal except in degenerate cases.
cards.originalText: The average price is lognormal only when the correlation between S(t) and Q(t) is zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Investors can take a synthetic long position in equity correlation by buying put options on an equity index and selling put options on the components of that index.
cards.explanation: Index volatility rises with correlation among the components. Long index options versus short component options therefore profit from rising correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The payoff for the buyer of a correlation swap is negative if the realized correlation of the underlying assets is higher than the fixed correlation in the swap.
cards.explanation: The buyer's payoff is positive when realized correlation exceeds the fixed rate.
cards.originalText: The payoff for the correlation buyer in a correlation swap is negative if the realized correlation of the underlying assets is higher than the fixed correlation in the swap.
cards.correction: The payoff for the buyer of a correlation swap is positive if the realized correlation of the underlying assets is higher than the fixed correlation in the swap.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The payoff to the buyer of a correlation swap is the notional multiplied by the difference between the realized and fixed variance of the index.
cards.explanation: A correlation swap pays on realized minus fixed correlation, not on variance.
cards.originalText: The payoff to the buyer of a correlation swap is the notional multiplied by the difference between realised and fixed variance of the index.
cards.correction: The payoff to the buyer of a correlation swap is the notional multiplied by the difference between the realized and fixed correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: In a systemic crisis correlations rise sharply, so correlation risk is greatest when diversification is most needed and diversification benefits shrink.
cards.explanation: Systemic stress pushes correlations up across assets, so diversification weakens exactly when it is most needed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A market-wide rise in correlation reflects company-specific factors, so diversification benefits are unchanged.
cards.explanation: A market-wide rise in correlation is driven by systematic factors, not company-specific ones, and it reduces diversification benefits.
cards.originalText: They are unrelated; the rise in correlation reflected company‑specific factors, so diversification benefits were unchanged.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A systemic crisis lowers correlations as investors rotate across asset classes, which increases diversification benefits.
cards.explanation: Correlations rise, not fall, in a crisis, which reduces diversification benefits.
cards.correction: A systemic crisis raises correlations as investors move together across asset classes, which reduces diversification benefits.

changes.to: raises correlations as investors move together

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For a creditor, the higher the concentration ratio, the higher the diversification and the lower the default risk.
cards.explanation: A high concentration ratio means concentrated exposure, less diversification and higher default risk.
cards.originalText: The higher the concentration ratio, the higher the diversification and the lower the default risk to the creditor.
cards.correction: For a creditor, the lower the concentration ratio, the higher the diversification and the lower the default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For a creditor, the lower the concentration ratio, the lower the diversification and the higher the default risk.
cards.explanation: The relationship is reversed: a lower concentration ratio means more diversification and lower default risk.
cards.originalText: The lower the concentration ratio, the lower the diversification and the higher the default risk to the creditor.
cards.correction: For a creditor, the lower the concentration ratio, the higher the diversification and the lower the default risk.

changes.from: lower the diversification and the higher the default risk
changes.to: higher the diversification and the lower the default risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: When the default correlation between loans is less than 1, a decrease in the concentration ratio decreases the joint probability of default.
cards.explanation: Spreading exposure over more borrowers lowers the probability that they all default together, provided default correlation is below 1.
cards.originalText: It will decrease.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: When the default correlation between loans is less than 1, a decrease in the concentration ratio increases the joint probability of default.
cards.explanation: More borrowers diversify the portfolio and lower, not raise, the joint probability of default.
cards.originalText: It will increase.
cards.correction: When the default correlation between loans is less than 1, a decrease in the concentration ratio decreases the joint probability of default.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The concentration ratio does not affect the joint probability of default.
cards.explanation: The concentration ratio is directly related to joint default probability. It has no effect only in the special case of a default correlation of 1.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: If the pairwise default correlation across all counterparties is 1, reducing the concentration ratio gives no reduction in joint default risk.
cards.explanation: At a default correlation of 1 all counterparties default together, so spreading exposure over more of them provides no diversification benefit.
cards.originalText: The ratio is 0.0455; if the pairwise default correlation across all counterparties were 1, reducing the ratio would give no reduction in joint default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Reducing the concentration ratio lowers the worst-case joint default probability irrespective of the level of default correlation.
cards.explanation: The benefit disappears at a default correlation of 1, when all counterparties default together and no diversification occurs.
cards.originalText: The ratio is 0.0455; reducing the ratio lowers the worst‑case joint default probability irrespective of the level of default correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In Tuckman's Model 1 ($dr = \sigma dw$), a change in the short-term rate shifts the predicted term structure of spot rates in parallel across all maturities.
cards.explanation: With a single factor and constant volatility, the predicted curve is the short rate minus a fixed convexity adjustment. A change in the short rate therefore moves every maturity equally, a recognised limitation versus observed non-parallel shifts.
cards.originalText: The whole term structure shifts up in parallel by about 20 basis points at every maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In Tuckman's Model 1, a rise in the short-term rate raises long-maturity rates by less than short-maturity rates because of mean reversion.
cards.explanation: Model 1 has no mean reversion; that feature belongs to the Vasicek model. In Model 1 the whole term structure shifts in parallel.
cards.originalText: Short‑maturity rates rise by 20 basis points but long‑maturity rates rise by less because of mean reversion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In Tuckman's Model 1, a rise in the short-term rate raises only the short end of the term structure and leaves long-maturity rates unchanged because the drift is zero.
cards.explanation: Long rates reflect expected future short rates, which are anchored to the current short rate in a zero-drift model. The whole curve therefore shifts in parallel.
cards.originalText: Only the short end rises by 20 basis points; long‑maturity rates are unchanged because the drift is zero.
