cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Tuckman's Model 1 implies a term structure that is perfectly flat at the current short rate for all maturities, including long maturities.
cards.explanation: With no drift, the convexity effect makes the predicted term structure of Model 1 downward-sloping at long maturities, so it is not flat.
cards.originalText: Model 1 implies a term structure that is perfectly flat at the current rate for all maturities, including the long‑term rates

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: A weakness of Tuckman's Model 1 (the normal model) is that the short-term rate can become negative.
cards.explanation: Rates in Model 1 are normally distributed, so negative rates are possible; this is the model's main drawback.
cards.originalText: A weakness of Model 1 (normal model) is that the short‑term rate can become negative

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Tuckman's Model 2 is more capable than Model 1 of producing an upward-sloping term structure, which is often observed.
cards.explanation: The constant drift (a risk premium) lets Model 2 generate an upward-sloping curve, whereas Model 1 has no drift.
cards.originalText: Model 2 is more capable of producing an upward‑sloping term structure, which is often observed

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Tuckman's Model 2 is an equilibrium model rather than an arbitrage-free model, because no attempt is made to match the term structure closely.
cards.explanation: Models 1 and 2 are not calibrated to match market prices, so they are equilibrium models. The Ho-Lee model is the first step toward arbitrage-free modeling.
cards.originalText: Model 2 is an equilibrium model rather than an arbitrage‑free model because no attempt is made to match the term structure closely

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In Tuckman's Model 1, a change in the short-term rate leads to a parallel shift in the predicted yield curve.
cards.explanation: Model 1 is a one-factor model, so any change in the short rate moves the whole predicted curve in parallel. This conflicts with observed non-parallel shifts.
cards.originalText: In Model 1, a change in the short‑term rate leads to a parallel shift in the predicted yield curve

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Tuckman's Model 1 predicts a hump-shaped term structure of volatility, consistent with observed volatility.
cards.explanation: Model 1 predicts a flat term structure of volatility, whereas observed volatility is hump-shaped.
cards.originalText: Model 1 predicts a hump‑shaped term structure of volatility, consistent with observed volatility

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Tuckman Model 2 tree is non-recombining because the drift is added only to the up-branches.
cards.explanation: The drift is added to all branches, which shifts the tree but keeps it recombining, because the up-down and down-up paths end at the same node.
cards.originalText: The Model 2 tree is non‑recombining because the drift is added only to the up‑branches

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct and describe the effectiveness of a short-term interest rate tree assuming normally distributed rates, both with and without drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The constant drift in Tuckman's Model 2 is easy to justify as an expected rate increase over very long horizons.
cards.explanation: Viewing the drift as an expected rate change is more defensible in the short run than over very long horizons.
cards.originalText: Model 2’s constant drift is easy to justify as an expected rate increase over very long horizons

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents a combination of the risk premium and the expected change in the short-term rate over that period.
cards.explanation: The drift is the sum of the expected rate change and the risk premium, which is why it is calibrated to market prices rather than estimated from forecasts.
cards.originalText: A combination of the risk premium and the expected change in the short‑term rate over that period

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents only the expected change in the short-term rate over that period.
cards.explanation: The drift also embeds the risk premium, so it is not purely an expected change in the rate.
cards.originalText: Only the expected change in the short‑term rate over that period
cards.correction: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents the expected change in the short-term rate and the risk premium over that period.

changes.from: only the expected change in the short-term rate
changes.to: the expected change in the short-term rate and the risk premium

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents only the risk premium demanded by investors over that period.
cards.explanation: The drift combines the risk premium with the expected change in the short-term rate; it is not the risk premium alone.
cards.originalText: Only the risk premium demanded by investors over that period
cards.correction: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents the risk premium and the expected change in the short-term rate over that period.

changes.from: only the risk premium demanded by investors
changes.to: the risk premium and the expected change in the short-term rate

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Construct a short-term rate tree under the Ho-Lee Model with time-dependent drift.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Ho-Lee model, the drift in a given period represents the expected change in the volatility of the short-term rate over that period.
cards.explanation: Drift and volatility are separate terms; volatility is the constant $\sigma$ term, while the drift reflects expected rate change and the risk premium.
cards.originalText: The expected change in the volatility of the short‑term rate over that period

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An approach that starts with assumptions about the interest rate process and the risk premium demanded by the market, and then derives the risk-neutral process, results in an equilibrium model.
cards.explanation: Equilibrium models start from assumptions about the true process and the risk premium and derive the risk-neutral process and prices. Arbitrage-free models start from observed market prices.
cards.originalText: An equilibrium model

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An approach that starts with assumptions about the interest rate process and the risk premium demanded by the market, and then derives the risk-neutral process, results in an arbitrage-free model.
cards.explanation: Arbitrage-free models take observed prices as input and back out the risk-neutral drift, which is the reverse direction.
cards.originalText: An arbitrage‑free model
cards.correction: An approach that starts with assumptions about the interest rate process and the risk premium demanded by the market, and then derives the risk-neutral process, results in an equilibrium model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: For an arbitrage-free interest rate model, understanding how the model's assumptions relate to the shape of the term structure lets the user interpret the assumptions about expectations, risk premium and volatility that the market is implicitly pricing.
cards.explanation: Because the model is fitted to the market, its parameters embody the market's implied assumptions. Understanding the link between assumptions and curve shape is how those assumptions are interpreted and sanity-checked.
cards.originalText: interpret the assumptions about expectations, risk premium and volatility that the market is implicitly pricing in the observed term structure

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In an arbitrage-free interest rate model, the true expected change in rates can be separated from the risk premium embedded in the calibrated drift.
cards.explanation: The calibrated drift is a blend of expected change and risk premium, and the two cannot be separated from prices alone.
cards.originalText: separate the true expected change in rates from the risk premium embedded in the calibrated drift

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An arbitrage-free interest rate model avoids the need to specify any process for the short-term rate, since the market curve replaces it.
cards.explanation: A process for the short rate is still required; calibration only fixes the drift so that the model matches market prices.
cards.originalText: avoid specifying any process for the short‑term rate, since the market curve replaces it

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An arbitrage-free interest rate model that reproduces observed market prices exactly confirms that those prices are fair.
cards.explanation: Matching prices does not show they are fair: the model itself may be bad, or market prices may be distorted, for example by forced liquidation.
cards.originalText: confirm that observed market prices are fair, because the model reproduces them exactly

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: According to Tuckman, the most important use of arbitrage-free interest rate models is quoting prices of illiquid or non-standard securities and valuing derivatives consistently with the prices of liquid securities.
cards.explanation: By matching liquid market prices, arbitrage-free models let dealers price illiquid or customized instruments and derivatives consistently with the market.
cards.originalText: Quoting prices of illiquid or non‑standard securities, and valuing derivatives, consistently with the prices of liquid securities

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Equilibrium models, rather than arbitrage-free models, are the appropriate choice for judging whether one bond is rich or cheap relative to another, because arbitrage-free models assume both securities are fairly priced.
cards.explanation: Arbitrage-free models take the fitted securities as correctly priced, so they cannot reveal relative mispricing. Equilibrium models are used for relative-value analysis.
cards.originalText: An equilibrium model, because arbitrage‑free models assume both securities are fairly priced and so cannot reveal relative mispricing

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: An arbitrage-free model is appropriate for judging whether one bond is rich or cheap relative to another, because calibrating to both bond prices makes their values directly comparable.
cards.explanation: Calibration builds in the assumption that both prices are right, so comparing the two reveals nothing about relative value.
cards.originalText: An arbitrage‑free model, because calibrating to both bond prices makes their values directly comparable

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Among Tuckman's Model 1, Model 2, Ho-Lee and Vasicek models, the Ho-Lee model is the easiest to fit to a wide variety of observed prices.
cards.explanation: Ho-Lee's time-dependent drift supplies one parameter per period, so it can be calibrated to a wide variety of market prices.
cards.originalText: Ho‑Lee

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the risk premium is indistinguishable from the long-run value of the short-term rate ($\theta$) when observing security prices.
cards.explanation: The risk premium is absorbed into the risk-neutral long-run rate, so it cannot be told apart from $\theta$ using observed prices.
cards.originalText: The risk premium is indistinguishable from the long‑run value of the short‑term rate ($\theta$) when observing security prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the risk premium directly affects the volatility of the short-term rate.
cards.explanation: The risk premium $\lambda$ shifts the drift only, and the volatility $\sigma$ is unchanged.
cards.originalText: The risk premium directly affects the volatility of the short‑term rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the risk premium affects only the short end of the yield curve and has no impact on long-term rates.
cards.explanation: The risk premium shifts the long-run level of the short rate, which feeds into the whole term structure.
cards.originalText: The risk premium only affects the short end of the yield curve and has no impact on long‑term rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Vasicek model incorporates mean reversion and models the risk premium as a component of the drift.
cards.explanation: Vasicek's drift is the mean-reverting term, and the risk premium enters as part of that drift.
cards.originalText: The model incorporates mean reversion and models the risk premium as a component of the drift.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Vasicek model incorporates mean reversion and a drift of zero.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion requires a non-zero drift; zero drift describes Tuckman's Model 1.
cards.originalText: The model incorporates mean reversion and a drift of zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Vasicek model has a drift of zero and cannot incorporate a risk premium.
cards.explanation: Zero drift describes Model 1. Vasicek includes a risk premium within its mean-reverting drift.
cards.originalText: The model incorporates a drift of zero, but it cannot incorporate a risk premium.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Vasicek model can model a time-varying risk premium but cannot incorporate mean reversion.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion is the defining feature of Vasicek, and its risk premium is constant rather than time-varying.
cards.originalText: The model can be used to model the time‑varying risk premium, but it cannot incorporate mean reversion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Due to mean reversion, it is impossible to develop a rate tree that recombines under the Vasicek model.
cards.explanation: A recombining approximation of the Vasicek tree exists, built by averaging the middle nodes and re-solving the probabilities.
cards.originalText: Due to the mean‑reversion, it is impossible to develop a rate tree that recombines under Vasicek

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Vasicek model is an equilibrium model like the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model and unlike the Ho-Lee model, which is an arbitrage-free model.
cards.explanation: Vasicek and CIR derive prices from assumptions about the rate process, whereas Ho-Lee is calibrated to match market prices.
cards.originalText: The Vasicek Model is an equilibrium model like the Cox‑Ingersoll‑Ross (CIR) model and unlike the Ho‑Lee model, which is an arbitrage‑free (aka, no‑arbitrage) model

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the half-life equals $\ln(2)/k$ and is the time it takes for the short rate to travel half the distance toward its long-run value $\theta$.
cards.explanation: With speed of mean reversion $k$, the gap between the rate and $\theta$ shrinks by half every $\ln(2)/k$ years.
cards.originalText: In the Vasicek Model, half‑life is given by LN(2)/k and can be interpreted as the time it takes for the short‑rate (the factor) to progress half the distance toward the long‑run value (Theta)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Mean reversion in the Vasicek model dampens volatility relative to the same process without mean reversion, particularly at long horizons.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion pulls rates back toward the long-run value, which produces a downward-sloping term structure of volatility.
cards.originalText: The mean reversion in Vasicek dampens volatility relative to the same process without mean reversion, particularly at long horizons

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the model $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma(t) dw$, the volatility of the short rate depends on time only, through the function $\sigma(t)$.
cards.explanation: The volatility coefficient is a deterministic function of time and contains no term in the rate $r$, so volatility varies only with time.
cards.originalText: Time only, through the function $\sigma(t)$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the model $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma(t) dw$, the volatility of the short rate depends on the current level of the short-term rate, as in the CIR model.
cards.explanation: Rate-level dependence belongs to models such as CIR ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$) and the lognormal model; here $\sigma(t)$ contains no $r$.
cards.originalText: The current level of the short‑term rate, as in the CIR model

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In the model $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma(t) dw$, the volatility of the short rate is constant, as in the Ho-Lee model.
cards.explanation: The function $\sigma(t)$ allows volatility to change over time, unlike the constant volatility of Ho-Lee.
cards.originalText: Neither the rate level nor time; volatility is a constant as in the Ho‑Lee model
cards.correction: In the model $dr = \lambda(t) dt + \sigma(t) dw$, the volatility of the short rate varies with time.

changes.from: is constant, as in the Ho-Lee model

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model has three mean-reverting factors that represent the short-, medium- and long-term levels of interest rates.
cards.explanation: Layered mean reversion at different speeds across the short-term, medium-term and long-term factors gives Gauss+ the flexibility to match observed rate and volatility behaviour.
cards.originalText: Three mean‑reverting factors representing the short‑, medium‑, and long‑term rate levels.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model has a single mean-reverting factor that captures only short-term dynamics.
cards.explanation: Gauss+ has three state variables (short, medium and long term). A single mean-reverting factor describes a one-factor model such as Vasicek.
cards.originalText: A single mean‑reverting factor capturing short‑term dynamics.
cards.correction: The Gauss+ model has three mean-reverting factors that capture short-, medium- and long-term dynamics.

changes.from: a single mean-reverting factor that captures only short-term dynamics
changes.to: three mean-reverting factors that capture short-, medium- and long-term dynamics

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The factors of the Gauss+ model are independent and non-mean-reverting.
cards.explanation: The Gauss+ factors are all mean-reverting and are linked in a cascade: the short rate reverts to the medium-term factor, which reverts to the long-term factor, which reverts to a fixed constant.
cards.originalText: Independent, non‑mean‑reverting factors that simplify modeling.
cards.correction: The factors of the Gauss+ model are linked in a cascade and are mean-reverting.

changes.to: linked in a cascade and are mean-reverting

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model can be calibrated to a hump-shaped volatility term structure: low volatility at the short end, higher volatility at medium maturities and declining volatility at long maturities.
cards.explanation: The short rate has no direct shock, so short-end volatility is low; the medium-term factor adds volatility at medium maturities and the slowly reverting long-term factor lets volatility decline at long maturities. This matches the hump observed in the market.
cards.originalText: Low volatility at the short end, higher volatility at medium maturities, and declining volatility at long maturities (hump‑shaped).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the short rate $r_t$ reverts directly to the constant $\mu$, bypassing the medium-term factor.
cards.explanation: The short rate reverts to the moving target $m_t$, which in turn reverts to $l_t$, which reverts to $\mu$; only $\mu$ is a fixed target.
cards.originalText: $r_{t}$ drifts down toward $\mu$ directly, bypassing $m_{t}$.
cards.correction: In the Gauss+ model, the short rate $r_t$ reverts to the medium-term factor $m_t$, not directly to the constant $\mu$.

changes.from: reverts directly to the constant $\mu$, bypassing the medium-term factor
changes.to: reverts to the medium-term factor $m_t$, not directly to the constant $\mu$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the short rate $r_t$ does not move because it has no random shock of its own.
cards.explanation: Having no shock is not the same as having no drift: the short rate still drifts toward the medium-term factor $m_t$, so it changes over time.
cards.originalText: $r_{t}$ does not move because it has no random shock.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the cascade form of the Gauss+ model, the short-term rate mean reverts to the medium-term factor, which in turn reverts to the long-term factor.
cards.explanation: Each factor chases the next one in the cascade, so the targets of the short-term and medium-term factors move over time. Only the long-term factor reverts to a fixed constant.
cards.originalText: In the cascade form, the short‑term rate mean reverts to the medium‑term factor, which reverts to the long‑term factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model has three state variables $r_t$, $m_t$ and $l_t$, denoting the short-term rate, a medium-term factor and a long-term factor.
cards.explanation: The three state variables form the cascade of the model: the short rate, a medium-term factor and a long-term factor.
cards.originalText: Gauss+ has three state variables $r_{t}$, $m_{t}$, $l_{t}$, denoting the short‑term rate, a medium‑term factor, and a long‑term factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the long-term factor mean reverts to a long-term constant level and reflects long-term trends such as inflation expectations and productivity.
cards.explanation: The long-term factor $l_t$ reverts to the fixed constant $\mu$ and captures slow-moving fundamentals such as inflation expectations and productivity.
cards.originalText: The long‑term factor mean reverts to a long‑term constant level and reflects long‑term trends such as inflation expectations and productivity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model is a cascade model in which each factor mean reverts to the next level.
cards.explanation: The short rate reverts to the medium-term factor, the medium-term factor reverts to the long-term factor, and the long-term factor reverts to the fixed constant $\mu$.
cards.originalText: A cascade model where each factor mean reverts to the next level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model is a single-factor model with constant volatility.
cards.explanation: Gauss+ has three factors with separate volatilities. A single-factor model with constant volatility is the Vasicek-type simplification.
cards.originalText: A single‑factor model with constant volatility.
cards.correction: The Gauss+ model is a three-factor model with separate factor volatilities.

changes.from: a single-factor model with constant volatility
changes.to: a three-factor model with separate factor volatilities

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model is a two-factor model with mean reversion to a fixed long-term rate.
cards.explanation: Gauss+ has three factors, not two, and only the constant $\mu$ is a fixed target; the other targets are moving factors.
cards.originalText: A two‑factor model with mean reversion to a fixed long‑term rate.
cards.correction: The Gauss+ model is a three-factor model with mean reversion to a fixed long-term rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the medium-term factor reflects economic influences such as business cycles.
cards.explanation: The medium-term factor is the moving target of the short rate and captures business-cycle-type influences and monetary policy effects.
cards.originalText: reflects economic influences, such as business cycles.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the medium-term factor remains constant over time.
cards.explanation: The medium-term factor $m_t$ is dynamic: it has its own drift toward the long-term factor and its own random shock.
cards.originalText: remains constant over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, the medium-term factor represents the risk premium in the interest rate structure.
cards.explanation: The Gauss+ factors are not risk premia; the medium-term factor captures broader economic influences such as business cycles and is the moving target for the short rate.
cards.originalText: represents the risk premium in the interest rate structure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the greater the difference between the short rate and the long-run level $\theta$, the greater the expected change in the short rate toward $\theta$.
cards.explanation: The expected change is the drift $k(\theta - r)dt$, which is proportional to the gap, so the pull toward $\theta$ strengthens as the gap widens.
cards.originalText: The greater the difference between $r$ and $\theta$, the greater the expected change in the short‑term rate towards $\theta$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the greater the difference between the short rate $r$ and $\theta$, the greater the value of the short rate.
cards.explanation: The gap can arise because $r$ is far above or far below $\theta$, so a larger gap does not imply a higher rate level; it implies a stronger pull toward $\theta$.
cards.originalText: The greater the difference between $r$ and $\theta$, the greater the value of the short‑term rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the speed of mean reversion $k$ increases as the difference between the short rate $r$ and $\theta$ increases.
cards.explanation: The speed of mean reversion $k$ is a fixed model parameter and does not depend on the current rate or on the gap between $r$ and $\theta$.
cards.originalText: The greater the difference between $r$ and $\theta$, the greater the value of $k$.
cards.correction: In the Vasicek model, the speed of mean reversion $k$ is a fixed parameter that does not change as the difference between the short rate $r$ and $\theta$ increases.

changes.from: increases as the difference between the short rate $r$ and $\theta$ increases
changes.to: is a fixed parameter that does not change as the difference between the short rate $r$ and $\theta$ increases

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the mean of the risk-neutral distribution of the short rate moves gradually from the current rate toward $\theta$, approaching $\theta$ as the horizon grows.
cards.explanation: The expected rate at horizon $T$ is $\theta + (r_0 - \theta)e^{-kT}$, so mean reversion pulls the mean gradually toward $\theta$ rather than instantly.
cards.originalText: The mean rises gradually from 2.0%, to about 3.2% at one year and about 4.8% at five years, approaching 5.0% as the horizon grows.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the mean of the short-rate distribution stays at the current rate at every horizon because the expected value of the random shock is zero.
cards.explanation: Only the shock has zero mean; the drift $k(\theta - r)$ moves the mean of the distribution toward $\theta$ over time.
cards.originalText: The mean stays at 2.0% at every horizon because the expected value of the random shock is zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the mean of the short-rate distribution jumps immediately to $\theta$ for any positive horizon and stays there.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion is gradual, governed by the speed $k$, so the mean converges toward $\theta$ as the horizon lengthens rather than jumping to it.
cards.originalText: The mean jumps immediately to 5.0% for any positive horizon and stays there.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model, the mean of the short-rate distribution rises without bound as the horizon lengthens because volatility accumulates over time.
cards.explanation: Volatility widens the distribution but does not move its mean; the mean converges to $\theta$.
cards.originalText: The mean rises without bound as the horizon lengthens because volatility accumulates over time.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In a short-rate model without mean reversion, the term structure of par-rate volatility is flat, whereas with mean reversion it declines with maturity.
cards.explanation: Without mean reversion a shock to the short rate moves all rates by about the same amount. With mean reversion, long rates reflect expected reversion, so shocks affect them less and volatility falls with maturity.
cards.originalText: Without mean reversion the volatility term structure is flat (shocks shift all rates alike); with mean reversion it declines with maturity, so the two are materially different.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In a short-rate model with mean reversion, long-maturity par-rate volatility is higher than short-maturity par-rate volatility.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion dampens the effect of shocks on long-term rates, so long-maturity volatility is lower, not higher, than short-maturity volatility.
cards.originalText: With mean reversion, long‑maturity par‑rate volatility is higher than short‑maturity volatility.
cards.correction: In a short-rate model with mean reversion, long-maturity par-rate volatility is lower than short-maturity par-rate volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: Calibrating the single volatility parameter of the Vasicek model to market volatility at one point on the curve will generally leave volatility mismatched at other maturities, which impairs derivative pricing and hedging.
cards.explanation: With one volatility parameter, the model structure fixes volatility at the other maturities and they will generally differ from the market. Gauss+ has several volatility parameters and a correlation and can fit the hump-shaped market volatility term structure.
cards.originalText: The model will generally mismatch market volatility at other maturities, impairing derivative pricing and hedging; Gauss+, with several volatility parameters and a correlation, can replicate a hump‑shaped volatility term structure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: Calibrating the volatility parameter of the Vasicek model to one point on the curve makes the model match market volatility at all other maturities.
cards.explanation: One volatility parameter fits only one point; the volatilities at other maturities are set by the model structure and will generally differ from the market.
cards.originalText: The model will automatically match market volatility at all other maturities; Gauss+ gives no improvement.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model focuses solely on short-term mean reversion, while the Gauss+ model incorporates multi-factor dynamics for short-, medium- and long-term rates.
cards.explanation: Vasicek is a single-factor short-rate model, whereas Gauss+ extends it to three cascading factors.
cards.originalText: The Vasicek model focuses solely on short‑term mean reversion, while the Gauss+ incorporates multi‑factor dynamics for short‑, medium‑, and long‑term rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model uses a multi-factor approach to capture complex rate dynamics.
cards.explanation: Vasicek is a single-factor model; the multi-factor model is Gauss+.
cards.originalText: The Vasicek model uses a multi‑factor approach to capture complex rate dynamics.
cards.correction: The Vasicek model uses a single-factor approach to capture rate dynamics.

changes.from: a multi-factor approach to capture complex rate dynamics
changes.to: a single-factor approach to capture rate dynamics

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model assumes a single-factor stochastic process with constant short-term volatility.
cards.explanation: Gauss+ has three factors and is not limited to one constant volatility level; its extra factors have their own volatilities.
cards.originalText: The Gauss+ model assumes a single‑factor stochastic process with constant short‑term volatility.
cards.correction: The Gauss+ model assumes a three-factor stochastic process with separate factor volatilities.

changes.from: a single-factor stochastic process with constant short-term volatility
changes.to: a three-factor stochastic process with separate factor volatilities

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The volatility parameters of the several Gauss+ factors, together with the correlation $\rho$, allow the model to produce low short-end volatility, higher mid-curve volatility and declining long-end volatility (a hump shape).
cards.explanation: Vasicek has one volatility parameter and calibrates volatility to a single point. Gauss+ has separate factor volatilities and a correlation, so it can fit the hump-shaped volatility term structure of the market.
cards.originalText: Its volatility parameters for the several factors and the correlation ρ allow low short‑end volatility, higher mid‑curve volatility and declining long‑end volatility (a hump shape).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model fixes one volatility level across all maturities, which makes the volatility structure easier to calibrate.
cards.explanation: A single volatility level across maturities is the Vasicek limitation. Gauss+ has several volatility parameters and can fit a hump-shaped volatility term structure.
cards.originalText: It fixes one volatility level across all maturities, making the volatility structure easier to calibrate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model contains stochastic volatility, which the Vasicek model lacks.
cards.explanation: Neither model has stochastic volatility: both use constant volatility parameters. Gauss+ fits market volatility better because it has several factors, not because volatility is stochastic.
cards.originalText: It contains stochastic volatility, which the Vasicek model lacks.
cards.correction: Neither the Gauss+ model nor the Vasicek model contains stochastic volatility.

changes.from: The Gauss+ model contains stochastic volatility, which the Vasicek model lacks
changes.to: Neither the Gauss+ model nor the Vasicek model contains stochastic volatility

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model the short rate reverts to a fixed $\theta$, whereas in the Gauss+ model $r$ reverts to $m$, $m$ reverts to $l$ and $l$ reverts to a fixed $\mu$, with reversion fastest for $r$ and slowest for $l$.
cards.explanation: Gauss+ replaces the single fixed target with a cascade of moving targets at different speeds, so only $\mu$ is fixed. This gives richer long-horizon dynamics than Vasicek.
cards.originalText: In Vasicek the short rate reverts to a fixed θ; in Gauss+ r reverts to m, m reverts to l, and l reverts to a fixed μ, with speeds fastest for r and slowest for l.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, all three factors revert directly to the fixed parameter $\mu$ at the same speed.
cards.explanation: The factors revert to each other in a cascade, not directly to $\mu$, and they do so at different speeds ($\alpha_r > \alpha_m > \alpha_l$).
cards.originalText: In Gauss+ all three factors revert to the fixed parameter μ at the same speed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Vasicek model the mean-reversion target moves dynamically, while in the Gauss+ model the target is fixed.
cards.explanation: It is the other way round: Vasicek has a single fixed target $\theta$, while Gauss+ has moving targets in a cascade and only the final target $\mu$ is fixed.
cards.originalText: In Vasicek the target moves dynamically, while in Gauss+ the target is fixed.
cards.correction: In the Gauss+ model the mean-reversion targets move dynamically, while in the Vasicek model the target is fixed.

changes.from: In the Vasicek model the mean-reversion target moves dynamically, while in the Gauss+ model the target is fixed
changes.to: In the Gauss+ model the mean-reversion targets move dynamically, while in the Vasicek model the target is fixed

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model offers little flexibility in the shape of the curve, so it cannot match market rates accurately enough for effective hedging across the yield curve.
cards.explanation: A single factor and a single volatility parameter restrict the curve shapes the model can produce; Gauss+ mitigates this with three factors.
cards.originalText: It offers little flexibility in the shape of the curve, so it cannot match market rates accurately enough for effective hedging.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model cannot price zero-coupon bonds in closed form.
cards.explanation: Vasicek does provide closed-form zero-coupon bond prices; this is one of its main uses.
cards.originalText: It cannot price zero‑coupon bonds in closed form.
cards.correction: The Vasicek model can price zero-coupon bonds in closed form.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model assumes volatility is stochastic.
cards.explanation: Vasicek assumes a constant volatility parameter, not stochastic volatility.
cards.originalText: It assumes volatility is stochastic, making hedge ratios unstable.
cards.correction: The Vasicek model assumes volatility is constant.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model has no mean reversion, so rates drift without an anchor.
cards.explanation: Mean reversion toward the long-run level $\theta$ is the defining feature of the Vasicek model.
cards.originalText: It has no mean reversion, so rates drift without anchor.
cards.correction: The Vasicek model has mean reversion, so rates are pulled toward an anchor.

changes.from: has no mean reversion, so rates drift without an anchor
changes.to: has mean reversion, so rates are pulled toward an anchor

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model assumes constant volatility, while the Gauss+ model can replicate hump-shaped volatility term structures.
cards.explanation: Vasicek has a single volatility parameter and cannot match the hump-shaped volatility term structure seen in the market. The multi-factor Gauss+ model can.
cards.originalText: The Vasicek model assumes constant volatility, while the Gauss+ model can replicate hump‑shaped volatility term structures.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: Both the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model have stochastic volatility components.
cards.explanation: Neither model has stochastic volatility. Both are Gaussian models with constant factor volatilities; the difference lies in the number of factors.
cards.originalText: Both models have stochastic volatility components.
cards.correction: Neither the Vasicek model nor the Gauss+ model has a stochastic volatility component.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model incorporates stochastic volatility, while the Gauss+ model assumes deterministic volatility.
cards.explanation: Vasicek does not have stochastic volatility, and Gauss+ is more flexible than Vasicek, not less: it can fit hump-shaped volatility term structures.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of options with a given maturity as a function of their strike price.
cards.explanation: Implied volatility is backed out of observed option prices with the Black-Scholes-Merton model; holding maturity fixed, it is plotted against the strike (or the strike divided by spot).
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with a given maturity as a function of its strike price.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of an option with an infinite life as a function of its current price.
cards.explanation: A smile requires a finite, fixed maturity, and the horizontal axis is the strike (or strike over spot), not the option price.
cards.originalText: The plot of the implied volatility of an option with an infinite life as a function of its current price.
cards.correction: A volatility smile is the plot of the implied volatility of options with a given maturity as a function of their strike price.

changes.from: of an option with an infinite life as a function of its current price
changes.to: of options with a given maturity as a function of their strike price

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A volatility smile is the pattern of changes in historical volatility across trading days for options with different expiration dates.
cards.explanation: A smile is built from implied, not historical, volatility and is plotted against strike for a fixed maturity, not against time or expiry.
cards.originalText: The pattern of changes in historical volatility across trading days for options with different expiration dates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: Implied volatility depends on the option pricing model used to invert the market price, so two traders using different models can obtain different implied volatilities from the same market price.
cards.explanation: Implied volatility is the volatility input that makes a model price equal the market price. Different models map volatility to price differently, so the implied volatility is model dependent.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities can differ, because implied volatility depends on the pricing model used to invert the market price.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: Two traders who use different option pricing models must obtain identical implied volatilities for the same option, because it is backed out of the same market price.
cards.explanation: The market price is common, but the inversion also depends on the pricing model, so different models generally give different implied volatilities.
cards.originalText: The implied volatilities must be identical, because they are backed out of the same market price.
cards.correction: Two traders who use different option pricing models can obtain different implied volatilities for the same option, even though it is backed out of the same market price.

changes.to: even though it is backed out

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: A hump-shaped plot of vega against the underlying price is not a volatility smile, because vega is a model-based sensitivity of option value to volatility whereas the smile plots implied volatility against strike (or strike over spot).
cards.explanation: The two plots show different objects. Under Black-Scholes-Merton, implied volatility would be flat across strikes while vega remains hump-shaped, highest for at-the-money options.
cards.originalText: It is not the smile: vega is a model‑based sensitivity of option value to volatility, whereas the smile plots implied volatility against strike (or K/S).

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: Under the Black-Scholes-Merton model, vega is the same for options of all strikes.
cards.explanation: Under Black-Scholes-Merton, vega is hump-shaped in the strike, highest for at-the-money options, even though implied volatility would be flat.
cards.originalText: It is not the smile, because under Black‑Scholes‑Merton vega would be constant across strikes, while implied volatility would be hump‑shaped.
cards.correction: Under the Black-Scholes-Merton model, vega is highest for at-the-money options and lower for options far from the money.

changes.from: is the same for options of all strikes
changes.to: is highest for at-the-money options and lower for options far from the money

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of the call equals that of the put, so their volatility smiles are identical.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity is a no-arbitrage identity that holds for market prices and for Black-Scholes-Merton prices alike, so the volatility that fits the call also fits the put.
cards.originalText: For the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of a European call equals that of a European put, so their volatility smiles are identical.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of the put is higher than that of the call whenever the underlying price distribution is not lognormal.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity is model-free and holds for non-lognormal distributions too; a different implied volatility for the put would create an arbitrage.
cards.originalText: For the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of a European put is higher than that of a European call whenever the underlying price distribution is not lognormal.
cards.correction: For European options with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of the put equals that of the call even when the underlying price distribution is not lognormal.

changes.from: is higher than that of the call whenever the underlying price distribution is not lognormal
changes.to: equals that of the call even when the underlying price distribution is not lognormal

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For European options with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of the call is higher than that of the put because calls have unlimited upside.
cards.explanation: Payoff asymmetry does not matter: put-call parity forces the call and the put to have the same implied volatility.
cards.originalText: For the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of a European call is higher than that of a European put because calls have unlimited upside.
cards.correction: For European options with the same strike and maturity, the implied volatility of the call equals that of the put even though calls have unlimited upside.

changes.from: is higher than that of the put because
changes.to: equals that of the put even though

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For European options on a non-dividend-paying stock with the same strike and maturity, put-call parity states that $c - p = S - PV(X)$.
cards.explanation: A fiduciary call (call plus $PV(X)$ in cash) and a protective put (stock plus put) have identical terminal payoffs, so $c + PV(X) = p + S$, which rearranges to $c - p = S - PV(X)$.
cards.originalText: $c - p = S - PV(X)$

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: For European options on a non-dividend-paying stock with the same strike and maturity, put-call parity states that $c + S = p + PV(X)$.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity equates a fiduciary call with a protective put: $c + PV(X) = p + S$. Pairing the call with the stock and the put with the bond gets the sign of $PV(X)$ wrong.
cards.originalText: $c + S = p + PV(X)$
cards.correction: For European options on a non-dividend-paying stock with the same strike and maturity, put-call parity states that $c + PV(X) = p + S$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: Put-call parity implies that a European call and put with the same underlying, strike and expiration have unequal implied volatilities, because puts and calls respond to volatility with opposite signs.
cards.explanation: Both calls and puts have positive vega, so volatility moves their prices in the same direction. Parity therefore forces equal implied volatilities for the call and put.
cards.originalText: unequal, because puts and calls respond to volatility with opposite signs
cards.correction: Put-call parity implies that a European call and put with the same underlying, strike and expiration have equal implied volatilities, because both respond to volatility with the same sign.

changes.from: unequal implied volatilities, because puts and calls respond to volatility with opposite signs
changes.to: equal implied volatilities, because both respond to volatility with the same sign

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: Put-call parity implies that a European call and put with the same underlying, strike and expiration have equal implied volatilities only if the options are at-the-money.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity applies at every strike, so the call and put have equal implied volatilities whatever their moneyness.
cards.originalText: equal only if the options are at‑the‑money
cards.correction: Put-call parity implies that a European call and put with the same underlying, strike and expiration have equal implied volatilities at any strike.

changes.from: only if the options are at-the-money

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If every option price in the market were consistent with the Black-Scholes-Merton model, implied volatility would be flat across strikes and the implied distribution of the terminal price would be lognormal.
cards.explanation: Constant-volatility geometric Brownian motion makes the terminal price lognormal, and one volatility prices every strike, so the implied volatility curve is flat.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility flat across strikes, and a lognormal implied distribution of the terminal price

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If every option price in the market were consistent with the Black-Scholes-Merton model, implied volatility would vary with strike while the implied distribution would still be lognormal.
cards.explanation: A strike-dependent implied volatility means the market-implied distribution differs from lognormal; a lognormal distribution corresponds to a flat implied volatility curve.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility that varies with strike but a lognormal implied distribution
cards.correction: If every option price in the market were consistent with the Black-Scholes-Merton model, implied volatility would be flat across strikes and the implied distribution would be lognormal.

changes.from: vary with strike while the implied distribution would still be lognormal
changes.to: be flat across strikes and the implied distribution would be lognormal

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If volatility is uncertain and positively correlated with the underlying price, out-of-the-money put options are priced lower, and in-the-money put options higher, than under constant volatility.
cards.explanation: Positive correlation gives a lighter left tail and a heavier right tail than lognormal. Low-strike options (out-of-the-money puts) become cheaper and high-strike options (in-the-money puts) become more expensive.
cards.originalText: Lower price for out‑of‑the‑money (OTM) put options and higher price for in‑the‑money (ITM) put options

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If volatility is uncertain and positively correlated with the underlying price, out-of-the-money call options are priced lower, and in-the-money call options higher, than under constant volatility.
cards.explanation: The pattern is reversed for calls: with positive correlation the right tail is heavier, so out-of-the-money (high-strike) calls are more expensive and in-the-money (low-strike) calls are cheaper.
cards.originalText: Lower price for out‑of‑the‑money (OTM) call options and higher price for in‑the‑money (ITM) call options
cards.correction: If volatility is uncertain and positively correlated with the underlying price, out-of-the-money call options are priced higher, and in-the-money call options lower, than under constant volatility.

changes.from: priced lower, and in-the-money call options higher
changes.to: priced higher, and in-the-money call options lower

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If the implied distribution has a lighter left tail and a heavier right tail than the lognormal distribution, the risk reversal (25-delta call implied volatility minus -25-delta put implied volatility) is positive.
cards.explanation: The 25-delta call sits in the heavy right tail and the -25-delta put in the light left tail, so the call implied volatility exceeds the put implied volatility.
cards.originalText: Positive risk reversal

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If the implied distribution has a lighter left tail and a heavier right tail than the lognormal distribution, the risk reversal (25-delta call implied volatility minus -25-delta put implied volatility) is negative.
cards.explanation: A negative risk reversal is the equity-style pattern of a heavier left tail. With a heavier right tail the call implied volatility is higher than the put implied volatility, so the risk reversal is positive.
cards.originalText: Negative risk reversal
cards.correction: If the implied distribution has a lighter left tail and a heavier right tail than the lognormal distribution, the risk reversal (25-delta call implied volatility minus -25-delta put implied volatility) is positive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: When implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as options move further in or out of the money (a smile), the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a heavier right tail than a lognormal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation.
cards.explanation: Elevated implied volatility at both low and high strikes means the market prices extreme moves in both directions above lognormal, as in currency options.
cards.originalText: The implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a heavier right tail.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: When implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as options move further in or out of the money (a smile), the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a less heavy right tail than a lognormal distribution.
cards.explanation: A smile has elevated implied volatility at both low and high strikes, so both tails are heavier than lognormal. A heavy left tail with a thin right tail describes the equity downward skew.
cards.originalText: The implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a less heavy right tail.
cards.correction: When implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as options move further in or out of the money (a smile), the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a heavier right tail than a lognormal distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: When implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as options move further in or out of the money (a smile), the implied distribution has a less heavy left tail and a less heavy right tail than a lognormal distribution.
cards.explanation: Lighter tails than lognormal give a frown, with implied volatility highest at the money. A smile corresponds to heavier tails on both sides.
cards.originalText: The implied distribution has a less heavy left tail and a less heavy right tail.
cards.correction: When implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as options move further in or out of the money (a smile), the implied distribution has a heavier left tail and a heavier right tail than a lognormal distribution.

changes.from: a less heavy left tail and a less heavy right tail
changes.to: a heavier left tail and a heavier right tail

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: An empirical distribution with a fatter right tail than a lognormal distribution implies greater implied volatilities for high strike prices.
cards.explanation: Implied volatility is higher at strikes where the true distribution has more probability mass than the lognormal, so a fat right tail raises implied volatility at high strikes.
cards.originalText: greater implied volatilities for high strike prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: An empirical distribution with a fatter right tail than a lognormal distribution implies greater implied volatilities for low strike prices.
cards.explanation: Greater implied volatility at low strikes describes a fatter left tail (the equity skew); a fatter right tail raises implied volatility at high strikes.
cards.originalText: greater implied volatilities for low strike prices.
cards.correction: An empirical distribution with a fatter right tail than a lognormal distribution implies greater implied volatilities for high strike prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: An empirical distribution with a fatter right tail than a lognormal distribution implies higher implied volatilities for mid-range strike prices.
cards.explanation: Elevated mid-range implied volatility would indicate light tails (a frown), not a fat right tail.
cards.originalText: higher implied volatilities for mid‑range strike prices.
cards.correction: An empirical distribution with a fatter right tail than a lognormal distribution implies higher implied volatilities for high strike prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
