cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: Compared with prices from a lognormal distribution, deep out-of-the-money calls priced from the volatility-smile-implied distribution are relatively cheap on an equity but relatively expensive on a foreign exchange rate.
cards.explanation: Equity options have a downward skew, so the right tail is thinner than lognormal and deep out-of-the-money calls are cheaper. The foreign exchange smile gives a fat right tail, so such calls are more expensive.
cards.originalText: The price of the option on ABC stock would be relatively low and the price of the option on USD/GBP FX rate would be relatively high compared to those computed from the lognormal counterparts.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: The risk reversal, defined as the 25-delta call implied volatility minus the -25-delta put implied volatility, is approximately equal to the implied volatility of the 50-delta (at-the-money) call.
cards.explanation: The risk reversal is a difference between two implied volatilities, not a level, so it measures skew and has no link to the at-the-money volatility.
cards.originalText: Risk reversal approximately equal to the implied volatility of the 50‑delta (at‑the‑money) call

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: As the maturity of options increases, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced.
cards.explanation: Both non-constant volatility and jumps have a smaller effect on implied volatility for long-dated options, so the smile flattens as maturity increases.
cards.originalText: When the maturity of options increases, the volatility smile becomes less pronounced.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: As the maturity of an option increases, the percentage impact of non-constant volatility on option prices becomes less pronounced.
cards.explanation: The percentage effect of non-constant volatility on option prices grows with maturity, although its effect on implied volatility usually shrinks.
cards.originalText: As the maturity of the option increases, the percentage impact of non‑constant volatility on prices becomes less pronounced.
cards.correction: As the maturity of an option increases, the percentage impact of non-constant volatility on option prices becomes more pronounced.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: The effects of variable volatility and jumps on option prices are independent of the maturity of the options.
cards.explanation: Both effects depend on maturity; their impact on the implied volatility smile is strongest for short-dated options.
cards.originalText: The effects of variable volatility and jumps are independent of the maturity of options.
cards.correction: The effects of variable volatility and jumps on the volatility smile depend on the maturity of the options.

changes.from: on option prices are independent of the maturity of the options
changes.to: on the volatility smile depend on the maturity of the options

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: If the actual price distribution has heavier left and right tails than the lognormal distribution assumed by Black-Scholes-Merton with constant volatility, a long strangle takes advantage of the mispricing.
cards.explanation: A long strangle buys out-of-the-money options in both tails; if these are underpriced because the market assumes lognormality, the position gains when extreme moves occur more often than the lognormal model implies.
cards.originalText: Long strangle

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: If the actual price distribution has heavier left and right tails than the lognormal distribution, a long butterfly spread takes advantage of the mispricing.
cards.explanation: A long butterfly is short the wings and profits when the price stays near the middle strike, the opposite of a fat-tail view.
cards.originalText: Long butterfly

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: If the actual price distribution has heavier left and right tails than the lognormal distribution, a short straddle takes advantage of the mispricing.
cards.explanation: A short straddle is short volatility and loses on large moves, so it is the opposite of a position that benefits from fat tails.
cards.originalText: Short straddle

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Crashophobia, the premium investors pay for out-of-the-money puts as protection against a sharp fall in equity prices, raises implied volatility at low strikes.
cards.explanation: Extra demand for crash protection bids up the prices of low-strike puts, which raises their implied volatilities and produces the equity skew.
cards.originalText: Crashophobia: investors pay a premium for out‑of‑the‑money puts as protection against a sharp fall in equity prices.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: A higher implied volatility for out-of-the-money equity puts is consistent with investors believing that the left tail of the price distribution is thinner than lognormal.
cards.explanation: A thinner left tail would make out-of-the-money puts cheaper and lower their implied volatility. High put implied volatility reflects a heavier left tail.
cards.originalText: Investors believe the left tail of the stock price distribution is thinner than lognormal.
cards.correction: A higher implied volatility for out-of-the-money equity puts is consistent with investors believing that the left tail of the price distribution is heavier than lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: A downward-sloping implied volatility skew is consistent with equity prices and volatility being negatively correlated.
cards.explanation: When volatility rises as the price falls, the left tail is heavier than lognormal, so low-strike options have higher implied volatility than high-strike options.
cards.originalText: Downward‑sloping skew; consistent with Peter’s assertion.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Demand for option protection against steep drops in equity prices leads to higher prices for out-of-the-money puts relative to out-of-the-money calls, creating a downward-sloping implied volatility skew.
cards.explanation: Persistent demand for downside protection (crashophobia) makes low-strike puts expensive, which produces the downward-sloping equity skew.
cards.originalText: Demand for option protection against steep drops in equity prices leads to higher prices in out‑of‑the‑money puts relative to out‑of‑the‑money calls, which creates a downward‑sloping implied volatility skew in these options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: The implied volatility smile commonly seen in foreign exchange options is due to a higher probability of a price change of between one and two standard deviations than would be expected under a lognormal distribution.
cards.explanation: The extra probability in foreign exchange rates is in the far tails; moves of one to two standard deviations are less likely than under a lognormal distribution.
cards.originalText: The implied volatility smile commonly seen in foreign exchange rate options is due to the higher probability of a price change of between one and two standard deviations from the mean than would be expected if prices are lognormally distributed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Demand for protection against unexpected central bank announcements leads to higher implied volatilities for at-the-money foreign exchange options than for out-of-the-money options.
cards.explanation: The foreign exchange smile has its lowest implied volatility at the money; a peak at the money would be a frown.
cards.originalText: Demand for option protection against the impact of unexpected central bank announcements on foreign exchange rates leads to higher prices, and higher implied volatilities, for at‑the‑money options relative to out‑of‑the‑money options.
cards.correction: Demand for protection against unexpected central bank announcements leads to higher implied volatilities for out-of-the-money foreign exchange options than for at-the-money options.

changes.from: for at-the-money foreign exchange options than for out-of-the-money options
changes.to: for out-of-the-money foreign exchange options than for at-the-money options

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Currency options have higher implied volatilities for deep in-the-money and deep out-of-the-money options and lower implied volatilities for at-the-money options.
cards.explanation: Both tails of the currency return distribution are heavier than lognormal, so implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises as the strike moves away in either direction (a smile).
cards.originalText: Currency options generate implied volatilities that are higher for deep‑in‑the‑money options and deep‑out‑of‑the‑money options and lower for at‑the‑money options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Currency options have higher implied volatilities for at-the-money options and lower implied volatilities for deep out-of-the-money and deep in-the-money options.
cards.explanation: That describes a frown (inverted smile), the pattern produced by a price jump or light tails; the usual currency pattern is a smile with the lowest volatility at the money.
cards.originalText: Currency options generate implied volatilities that are higher for at‑the‑money options and lower for deep‑out‑of‑the‑money and deep‑in‑the‑money options.
cards.correction: Currency options have lower implied volatilities for at-the-money options and higher implied volatilities for deep out-of-the-money and deep in-the-money options.

changes.from: higher implied volatilities for at-the-money options and lower implied volatilities for deep out-of-the-money and deep in-the-money options
changes.to: lower implied volatilities for at-the-money options and higher implied volatilities for deep out-of-the-money and deep in-the-money options

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Currency options have higher implied volatilities for deep in-the-money options and lower implied volatilities for deep out-of-the-money options.
cards.explanation: That is a one-sided downward skew, typical of equity options. The currency smile is roughly symmetric, with elevated volatility for deep out-of-the-money options too.
cards.originalText: Currency options generate implied volatilities that are higher for deep‑in‑the‑money options and lower for deep‑out‑of‑the‑money options.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Increased demand for downside tail-risk protection raises implied volatility at low strikes and steepens the equity volatility skew.
cards.explanation: Greater demand for crash protection bids up low-strike put prices and implied volatilities, steepening the downward-sloping left-hand skew characteristic of equity options.
cards.originalText: Demand for downside tail‑risk protection increases, raising implied volatility at low strikes and steepening the skew.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Higher demand for out-of-the-money equity puts raises implied volatility at high strikes, so the skew becomes upward-sloping.
cards.explanation: Out-of-the-money puts have low strikes, so the extra demand raises implied volatility at low strikes and makes the skew more downward-sloping.
cards.originalText: Higher demand for OTM puts raises implied volatility at high strikes, so the skew becomes an upward‑sloping smirk.
cards.correction: Higher demand for out-of-the-money equity puts raises implied volatility at low strikes, so the skew becomes more downward-sloping.

changes.from: at high strikes, so the skew becomes upward-sloping
changes.to: at low strikes, so the skew becomes more downward-sloping

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Increasing leverage at lower equity prices suggests that equity volatility increases as the stock price falls.
cards.explanation: When the equity value falls, debt-to-equity rises and the stock becomes riskier, so volatility rises as price falls. This supports higher implied volatility at low strikes.
cards.originalText: Increasing leverage at lower equity prices suggests increasing volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the volatility smile for equity options and foreign currency options and provide possible explanations for its shape.
cards.statement: Compared with the lognormal distribution, equity option traders believe the probability of large down moves in price is similar to the probability of large up moves.
cards.explanation: Traders treat large down moves as more probable than large up moves, giving a left-skewed implied distribution; that is why equity options show a skew.
cards.originalText: Compared to the lognormal distribution, traders believe the probability of large down movements in price is similar to large up movements.
cards.correction: Compared with the lognormal distribution, equity option traders believe the probability of large down moves in price is greater than the probability of large up moves.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: VaR gives a loss threshold but says nothing about the size of losses beyond it, whereas expected shortfall measures the expected loss given that the threshold is exceeded.
cards.explanation: This is the central motivation for the move to expected shortfall: it captures tail severity, which VaR ignores.
cards.originalText: VaR gives a loss threshold but says nothing about the size of losses beyond it, whereas ES measures the expected loss given that the threshold is exceeded.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: For a normal distribution, 97.5% expected shortfall (mean plus 2.338 standard deviations) is almost identical to 99% VaR (mean plus 2.326 standard deviations), but the two can differ considerably when tails are fat.
cards.explanation: The near-equivalence under normality is why the FRTB lowered the confidence level to 97.5% when it moved to expected shortfall.
cards.originalText: For a normal distribution, 97.5% ES (mean plus 2.338 standard deviations) is almost identical to 99% VaR (mean plus 2.326 standard deviations), but the two can differ considerably when tails are fat.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is easier to backtest than VaR, which is why the FRTB requires the stressed expected shortfall itself to be backtested.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall is harder to backtest than VaR, and the stressed expected shortfall cannot be backtested because stressed extremes need not recur with the same frequency.
cards.originalText: ES is easier to backtest than VaR, which is why the FRTB requires the stressed ES itself to be backtested.
cards.correction: Expected shortfall is harder to backtest than VaR, which is why the FRTB does not require the stressed expected shortfall itself to be backtested.

changes.from: easier to backtest than VaR, which is why the FRTB requires
changes.to: harder to backtest than VaR, which is why the FRTB does not require

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB bases capital on a single expected shortfall calibrated to a stressed period, rather than adding a current 10-day VaR to a stressed VaR.
cards.explanation: The Basel II.5 sum of current VaR and stressed VaR is replaced by one stressed expected shortfall.
cards.originalText: The FRTB bases capital on a single ES calibrated to a stressed period, rather than adding a current 10‑day VaR to a stressed VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, market risk capital is measured with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level, replacing 99% VaR.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall captures tail severity and, for a normal distribution, 97.5% expected shortfall gives about the same capital as 99% VaR (2.338 versus 2.326 standard deviations).
cards.originalText: Expected shortfall with a 97.5% confidence level

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, market risk capital is measured with expected shortfall at a 99% confidence level.
cards.explanation: The FRTB uses a 97.5% confidence level for expected shortfall; 99% was the confidence level of the VaR it replaced.
cards.originalText: Expected shortfall with a 99% confidence level
cards.correction: Under the FRTB, market risk capital is measured with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, market risk capital is measured with VaR at a 99% confidence level.
cards.explanation: 99% VaR is the pre-FRTB measure; the FRTB replaces it with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.
cards.originalText: VaR at 99% confidence
cards.correction: Under the FRTB, market risk capital is measured with expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level.

changes.to: expected shortfall at a 97.5% confidence level

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Basel I and Basel II.5 used a 10-day horizon for all risk factors, whereas the FRTB uses five liquidity horizons (10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days) depending on the liquidity of the risk factor.
cards.explanation: Under the FRTB, less liquid risk factors are assigned longer liquidity horizons, replacing the single 10-day horizon.
cards.originalText: Basel I and Basel II.5 used a 10‑day horizon for all risk factors, whereas the FRTB uses five liquidity horizons (10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days) depending on the liquidity of the risk factor.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Basel II.5 required a default-related charge for credit-dependent positions, but the FRTB eliminates any such charge and relies on VaR and expected shortfall alone.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with an incremental default risk charge (99.9% VaR, one-year horizon), so a default charge remains.
cards.originalText: Basel II.5 required a default‑related charge for credit‑dependent positions, but the FRTB eliminates any such charge and relies on VaR and ES alone.
cards.correction: Basel II.5 required a default-related charge for credit-dependent positions, and the FRTB replaces it with an incremental default risk charge.

changes.from: but the FRTB eliminates any such charge and relies on VaR and expected shortfall alone
changes.to: and the FRTB replaces it with an incremental default risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB requires a stressed expected shortfall measure to be used in determining market risk capital, rather than the VaR and stressed VaR used under Basel II.5.
cards.explanation: The defining change is a single stressed expected shortfall at 97.5% confidence replacing the combination of VaR and stressed VaR.
cards.originalText: FRTB requires that the stressed ES measure be used in determining market risk capital, rather than the VaR and stressed VaR that were used in Basel I and Basel II.5.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Basel I and Basel II.5 allowed market risk to be calculated at the trading desk level, whereas the FRTB requires market risk to be calculated on a firm-wide basis.
cards.explanation: It is reversed: the FRTB introduces desk-level model approval and calculation, whereas Basel I and Basel II.5 worked on a firm-wide basis.
cards.originalText: While Basel I and Basel II.5 allowed market risk to be calculated at the trading desk level, FRTB requires that market risk be calculated on a firm‑wide basis.
cards.correction: Basel I and Basel II.5 calculated market risk on a firm-wide basis, whereas the FRTB introduces desk-level model approval and calculation.

changes.from: allowed market risk to be calculated at the trading desk level, whereas the FRTB requires market risk to be calculated on a firm-wide basis
changes.to: calculated market risk on a firm-wide basis, whereas the FRTB introduces desk-level model approval and calculation

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardizes the liquidity horizon for all risk factors in the market risk capital calculation at 10 days, rather than the different horizons used in Basel I and Basel II.5.
cards.explanation: The uniform 10-day horizon is the old approach. The FRTB uses five liquidity horizons (10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days) depending on the liquidity of the risk factor.
cards.originalText: FRTB standardizes the liquidity horizon for all risk factors in the market risk capital calculation as 10 days, rather than the different horizons used in Basel I and Basel II.5.
cards.correction: The FRTB uses different liquidity horizons for different risk factors in the market risk capital calculation, rather than the uniform 10-day horizon used in Basel I and Basel II.5.

changes.from: standardizes the liquidity horizon for all risk factors in the market risk capital calculation at 10 days, rather than the different horizons used in Basel I and Basel II.5
changes.to: uses different liquidity horizons for different risk factors in the market risk capital calculation, rather than the uniform 10-day horizon used in Basel I and Basel II.5

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Both Basel I and Basel II.5 require the calculation of VaR at a 99% confidence level.
cards.explanation: Both regimes use 99% VaR; Basel II.5 added a stressed VaR on top of it.
cards.originalText: Both Basel I and Basel II.5 require calculation of VaR with a 99% confidence level.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB requires adding a stressed VaR measure to complement the expected shortfall calculation.
cards.explanation: The stressed VaR add-on belongs to Basel II.5. The FRTB drops the VaR plus stressed VaR combination and uses a stressed-period expected shortfall alone.
cards.originalText: FRTB requires adding a stressed VaR measure to complement the expected shortfall calculation.
cards.correction: The FRTB does not add a stressed VaR measure to complement the expected shortfall calculation.

changes.from: requires adding a stressed VaR measure
changes.to: does not add a stressed VaR measure

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The 10-day VaR used for market risk capital under Basel I is a current measure that uses a recent period of data, typically one to four years.
cards.explanation: Because it is based on recent data, the Basel I 10-day 99% VaR reflects current market conditions.
cards.originalText: The 10‑day time horizon for market risk capital proposed under Basel I incorporates a recent period of time, which typically ranges from one to four years.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Funding risk is a risk class under the sensitivities-based method of the FRTB standardized approach.
cards.explanation: The sensitivities-based method has seven risk classes: general interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity, equity and three credit spread classes. Funding risk is not among them.
cards.originalText: Funding risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: General interest rate risk is a risk class under the sensitivities-based method of the FRTB standardized approach.
cards.explanation: General interest rate risk is one of the seven risk classes of the sensitivities-based method.
cards.originalText: General interest rate risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Commodity risk is a risk class under the sensitivities-based method of the FRTB standardized approach.
cards.explanation: Commodity risk is one of the seven risk classes of the sensitivities-based method.
cards.originalText: Commodity risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a risk charge calculated with a sensitivities-based method.
cards.explanation: The FRTB standardized capital charge is the sum of a sensitivities-based risk charge, a default risk charge and a residual risk add-on.
cards.originalText: A risk charge calculated using a risk sensitivity approach

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a residual risk add-on.
cards.explanation: The residual risk add-on captures exotic and other risks not covered by the sensitivities-based method; it is one of the three components of the standardized charge.
cards.originalText: A residual risk add‑on

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes a default risk charge.
cards.explanation: The default risk charge, which captures jump-to-default risk, is one of the three components of the FRTB standardized charge.
cards.originalText: A default risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Describe the changes to the Basel framework for calculating market risk capital under the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) and the motivations for these changes.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardized approach includes an insolvency risk charge as one of its components.
cards.explanation: The standardized charge has exactly three components: the sensitivities-based risk charge, the default risk charge and the residual risk add-on. There is no insolvency risk charge.
cards.originalText: Insolvency risk charge

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time required to sell a security in a stressed market without materially affecting market prices.
cards.explanation: A liquidity horizon is the period, assessed in stressed market conditions, that it takes to exit a risk factor exposure without materially moving the market. Longer horizons (10 to 120 days) imply larger capital.
cards.originalText: The time required to sell a security in a stressed market, without materially affecting market prices

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time taken to find a willing buyer for a security or commodity.
cards.explanation: Finding a buyer is only part of an exit. The liquidity horizon is the time needed to complete the sale or hedge in stressed conditions without materially affecting prices.
cards.originalText: The time taken to find a willing buyer for a security or commodity

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time taken to execute a sale that guarantees a minimum level of profit.
cards.explanation: A liquidity horizon concerns how long it takes to exit an exposure in stressed markets without moving prices. It has nothing to do with guaranteeing a profit.
cards.originalText: The time taken to successfully execute a sale transaction that guarantees a minimum level of profit

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a liquidity horizon is the time it takes to buy a security or commodity.
cards.explanation: The liquidity horizon concerns exiting or hedging an existing exposure in stressed markets, not buying a position.
cards.originalText: The time it takes to buy a security or commodity

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10-day shock to liquidity-horizon categories j through 5 only, each ES$_{j}$ (j ≥ 2) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms because the horizons are treated as independent.
cards.explanation: The cascade removes lower-horizon categories step by step and scales each incremental horizon by the square-root rule. Because shocks in different horizon buckets are assumed independent, the pieces are aggregated in quadrature.
cards.originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, holding categories 1 to j‑1 constant. Each ES$_{j}$ (j ≥ 2) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms, reflecting independence across horizons.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, the five cascade terms are added together in a simple sum because changes in the risk factor groups are assumed perfectly correlated.
cards.explanation: The FRTB formula assumes the horizon buckets are independent and combines the cascade terms as the square root of the sum of squares, not as a simple sum.
cards.originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, but total ES is the simple sum of the five terms because variable changes are assumed perfectly correlated, the most conservative assumption.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, each cascade term ES$_{j}$ is scaled by $\sqrt{LH_{j}/10}$, using the full liquidity horizon rather than the incremental horizon.
cards.explanation: Each term is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, the incremental horizon. Using the full horizon would double count time already covered by the lower-numbered ES terms.
cards.originalText: ES$_{j}$ is the ES from a 10‑day shock to categories j through 5 only, but each is scaled by $\sqrt{LH_{j}/10}$ (the full horizon), and total ES is the square root of the sum of the squared terms.
cards.correction: In the FRTB liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall, each cascade term ES$_{j}$ is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_{j} - LH_{j-1})/10}$, using the incremental liquidity horizon rather than the full horizon.

changes.from: using the full liquidity horizon rather than the incremental horizon
changes.to: using the incremental liquidity horizon rather than the full horizon

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB computes liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall once from a 10-day shock to all risk factors and multiplies it by $\sqrt{120/10}$, so that every risk factor is treated as having the longest liquidity horizon.
cards.explanation: The FRTB assigns each risk factor its own liquidity horizon through the cascade of nested ES calculations. Scaling everything by the longest horizon would be far more punitive and is not the FRTB method.
cards.originalText: ES is computed once from a 10‑day shock to all risk factors and then multiplied by $\sqrt{120/10}$, so that every risk factor is treated as if it had the longest liquidity horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB standardized approach, liquidity horizons of risk factors are incorporated into market risk capital through the risk weights determined by the Basel Committee.
cards.explanation: The Basel Committee sets the standardized risk weights so that they reflect each risk factor's liquidity horizon: longer horizons lead to larger risk weights.
cards.originalText: Under the standardized approach, the liquidity horizons of risk factors are incorporated into market risk capital calculations through the risk weights determined by the Basel Committee.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB standardized approach incorporates diversification benefits between risk factors with different liquidity horizons through the risk weights set by the Basel Committee.
cards.explanation: Risk weights reflect liquidity horizons, not diversification. Diversification benefits in the standardized approach come from the prescribed correlation assumptions.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach incorporates the diversification benefits between risk factors with different liquidity horizons through the risk weights set by the Basel Committee.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB historical simulation approach, liquidity-adjusted expected shortfall is estimated by assuming a 10-day liquidity horizon for all risk factors, because their behaviour is highly correlated in volatile markets.
cards.explanation: The liquidity-adjusted ES uses five liquidity horizons (10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days) in a cascade. A single uniform 10-day horizon is not assumed for every risk factor.
cards.originalText: The historical simulation approach estimates a liquidity‑adjusted ES by assuming a 10‑day liquidity horizon for all risk factors, since their behavior will most likely be highly correlated during volatile market conditions.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, expected shortfall is based on a waterfall (cascade) of liquidity-horizon categories, with each nested ES scaled by the square root of the difference between successive horizon lengths.
cards.explanation: The IMA computes ES from nested 10-day shocks by liquidity-horizon category and combines them using the square root of the differences between successive horizon lengths, assuming behaviour in each further period is independent.
cards.originalText: The expected shortfall is based on a waterfall of the liquidity horizon categories and is then scaled to the square root of the difference in the horizon lengths of the nested risk factors.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Compare the various liquidity horizons proposed by the FRTB for different asset classes and explain how a bank can calculate its expected shortfall using the various horizons.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, liquidity horizons are brought into expected shortfall through a series of weights together with a correlation factor determined by the Basel Committee.
cards.explanation: The IMA assumes independence across liquidity-horizon categories and uses the square-root rule on incremental horizons. There is no regulatory correlation parameter and no weighting scheme.
cards.originalText: A series of weights is applied to the various liquidity horizons along with a correlation factor determined by the Basel Committee.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB requires no market risk capital charge for jump-to-default risk, because default exposures are charged only under the credit risk rules of the banking book.
cards.explanation: Jump-to-default risk is explicitly charged within the trading book under market risk capital, through the default risk charge (internal models: 99.9% VaR over one year).
cards.originalText: The FRTB requires no market risk capital charge for jump‑to‑default risk, because default exposures are charged only under the credit risk rules of the banking book.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, credit spread risk, the risk that a change in the credit spread alters the mark-to-market value of a position, can be addressed within the expected shortfall calculation.
cards.explanation: Credit spread risk is treated like other market risk factors and is captured in the expected shortfall process, with liquidity horizons of 20 to 120 days.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk, the risk that a change in the credit spread alters mark‑to‑market value, can be addressed within the expected shortfall calculation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk is subject to a capital charge calculated as a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
cards.explanation: Jump-to-default risk is handled like banking book default risk, with a 99.9% VaR over one year. These numbers are often confused with the 97.5% ES used for market risk factors.
cards.originalText: Jump‑to‑default risk is subject to the incremental default risk (IDR) charge, calculated as a 99.9% VaR with a one‑year horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, the liquidity horizon for credit spreads ranges from 20 to 120 days, and the liquidity horizon for credit spread volatility is 120 days.
cards.explanation: Credit spread liquidity horizons run from 20 days (for example investment-grade sovereigns) to 120 days (other credit spreads), and credit spread volatility has a horizon of 120 days.
cards.originalText: Under the internal models approach, the liquidity horizon for credit spreads ranges from 20 to 120 days, and the liquidity horizon for credit spread volatility is 120 days.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a one-day horizon.
cards.explanation: Backtesting compares daily P&L with one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months, which gives enough observations for a meaningful exception count.
cards.originalText: One‑day horizon

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a thirty-day horizon.
cards.explanation: A thirty-day horizon would leave too few non-overlapping observations in 12 months. The FRTB backtests one-day VaR.
cards.originalText: Thirty‑day horizon

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests value at risk using a two-day horizon.
cards.explanation: Two days has no basis in the FRTB. Backtesting uses a one-day VaR horizon.
cards.originalText: Two‑day horizon

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Instruments in the trading book are marked to market.
cards.explanation: Trading book instruments are periodically marked to market, whereas banking book instruments are not marked to market in the same way.
cards.originalText: Instruments in the trading book

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, trading book instruments are valued using historical cost accounting.
cards.explanation: Trading book instruments are marked to market. Historical cost valuation is associated with the banking book.
cards.originalText: Instruments in the trading book are valued using historical cost accounting

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.
cards.explanation: Credit spread risk (a change in the company's spread changes mark-to-market value) is handled with expected shortfall, while jump-to-default risk (the company defaults) has its own default risk charge.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk and jump‑to‑default risk

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and interest rate risk.
cards.explanation: Interest rate risk is a general market risk factor captured in the standard ES. The two credit-specific exposures are credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk and interest rate risk
cards.correction: The FRTB distinguishes two types of credit risk exposure to a company: credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests a one-day VaR rather than the stressed ES capital measure, because ES is harder to backtest than VaR and a stressed measure cannot be backtested since stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency.
cards.explanation: The capital measure is stressed expected shortfall, which cannot be backtested directly. The FRTB therefore backtests a one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months instead.
cards.originalText: Expected shortfall is harder to backtest than VaR, and a stressed measure cannot be backtested because stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Value at risk is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not.
cards.explanation: It is the other way round: VaR is not subadditive and so is not coherent, while expected shortfall is coherent.
cards.originalText: VaR at the 99% level is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not, so only VaR can be validated
cards.correction: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure whereas value at risk is not.

changes.from: Value at risk is a coherent risk measure whereas expected shortfall is not
changes.to: Expected shortfall is a coherent risk measure whereas value at risk is not

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, the capital charge for market risk is itself based on a one-day 99% VaR.
cards.explanation: The FRTB capital charge is based on a stressed 97.5% expected shortfall with liquidity horizons of 10 to 120 days. One-day VaR is used only for backtesting.
cards.originalText: The FRTB capital charge is itself based on one‑day 99% VaR, so the same measure must be backtested

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, all risk factors have a one-day liquidity horizon.
cards.explanation: FRTB liquidity horizons range from 10 to 120 days, not one day.
cards.originalText: All risk factors under the FRTB have a one‑day liquidity horizon, so one‑day VaR matches the capital measure

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB tightens the rules separating the trading book from the banking book because banks could lower capital by placing credit-dependent assets in whichever book carried the lower requirement.
cards.explanation: The boundary determines which capital regime applies (market risk versus credit risk rules), creating an incentive for regulatory arbitrage that the FRTB aims to remove.
cards.originalText: Banks could lower capital by placing credit‑dependent assets in whichever book carried the lower requirement

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB backtests one-day value at risk at both the 97.5% and the 99.0% confidence levels.
cards.explanation: Because stressed ES cannot be backtested, the FRTB backtests one-day VaR at both confidence levels over the most recent 12 months.
cards.originalText: One‑day value at risk (VaR) is backtested at both 97.5% and 99.0% confidence levels

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: FRTB backtesting consists of two tests: a 10-day 99.0% expected shortfall test and a 10-day 99.0% stressed value at risk test.
cards.explanation: Stressed measures are not backtested and the backtesting horizon is one day. The FRTB backtests one-day VaR at the 97.5% and 99.0% confidence levels.
cards.originalText: There are two tests: 10‑day 99.0% expected shortfall and 10‑day 99.0% stressed value at risk (sVaR)

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary between the trading and banking books, including assignment when a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books.
cards.explanation: The FRTB keeps two books but tightens the boundary with objective criteria, assignment at inception and strict limits on switching, to reduce regulatory arbitrage.
cards.originalText: The FRTB establishes a more objective boundary, including assignment when a position is initiated and strict limits on subsequent movement between the books

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB collapses the banking book and the trading book into a single book.
cards.explanation: The FRTB retains two separate books with different capital frameworks. It tightens the boundary between them rather than merging them.
cards.originalText: The FRTB collapses the banking and trading books into a single book, which solves the regulatory arbitrage problem

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, a sincere intent to trade is necessary and sufficient for a position to be included in the trading book.
cards.explanation: Intent to trade alone is no longer sufficient. The bank must also be able to trade the asset and manage its risks on a trading desk.
cards.originalText: The FRTB says that a sincere ”intent to trade” is necessary and sufficient for trading‑book inclusion; moving a position between books triggers the incremental risk charge as a penalty

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB requires backtesting to be performed on the 97.5% stressed expected shortfall used for the capital charge, with a 10-day horizon.
cards.explanation: The FRTB never backtests the stressed ES capital measure. It backtests a one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months.
cards.originalText: The backtest must be performed on the 97.5% stressed ES used for the capital charge, with a 10‑day horizon

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, stressed expected shortfall measures are not backtested because extreme stressed values may not recur with the same frequency.
cards.explanation: A stressed measure cannot be backtested meaningfully because stressed data are not expected to recur with the same frequency. Expected shortfall is also harder to backtest than VaR.
cards.originalText: Stressed expected shortfall measures are not backtested because extreme stressed values may not recur with the same frequency

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: FRTB backtesting uses a one-day horizon and the latest 12 months of data.
cards.explanation: The FRTB backtests one-day VaR over the most recent 12 months.
cards.originalText: Backtesting uses a one‑day horizon and the latest 12 months of data

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under FRTB backtesting at the 99% confidence level, more than 12 exceptions in the 12-month period requires the desk to use the standardized approach.
cards.explanation: The thresholds are more than 12 exceptions at the 99% level or more than 30 exceptions at the 97.5% level; breaching either forces the desk onto the standardized approach.
cards.originalText: At the 99% level, more than 12 exceptions in the period requires the standardized approach

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with a default risk charge that recognizes jump-to-default risk and includes equity products.
cards.explanation: The default risk charge explicitly captures jump-to-default risk and, unlike the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge, also covers equity positions.
cards.originalText: The FRTB replaces the IRC with a default risk charge (DRC), which recognizes jump‑to‑default risk and mandates the inclusion of equity products

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The FRTB makes no changes to the incremental risk charge introduced under Basel II.5.
cards.explanation: The FRTB replaces the incremental risk charge with a default risk charge (99.9% VaR over one year) that recognizes jump-to-default risk.
cards.originalText: The FRTB makes no changes to the IRC

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: The default risk charge that replaces the incremental risk charge under the FRTB does not recognize jump-to-default risk and explicitly excludes equity products.
cards.explanation: The default risk charge exists to capture jump-to-default risk, and it includes equity products. The statement reverses both features.
cards.originalText: The FRTB replaces the IRC with a default risk charge (DRC), which does not recognize jump‑to‑default risk and explicitly excludes equity products

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.
cards.explanation: Transfers are allowed only in extraordinary circumstances such as the closing of a trading desk or a change in accounting standards, and any resulting capital benefit is disallowed, which removes the incentive to switch books.
cards.originalText: Reclassification is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category.
cards.explanation: Even when a transfer is allowed in extraordinary circumstances, any capital benefit from moving the position between the books is disallowed.
cards.originalText: Reclassification is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category.
cards.correction: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is permitted only in extraordinary circumstances, and any capital benefit from the move is disallowed.

changes.from: the bank keeps the full capital benefit of the new category
changes.to: any capital benefit from the move is disallowed

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, reclassification of a position between the trading book and the banking book is never permitted under any circumstances.
cards.explanation: Transfers are allowed in extraordinary circumstances, such as the closing of a trading desk or a change in accounting standards on fair value recognition, but any capital benefit is disallowed.
cards.originalText: Reclassification is never permitted under any circumstances.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
cards.explanation: Jump-to-default risk is treated like banking book default risk, using a 99.9% VaR over one year, whereas credit spread risk is handled through expected shortfall.
cards.originalText: Jump‑to‑default risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB internal models approach, credit spread risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.
cards.explanation: Credit spread risk is handled like other market risks, with 97.5% stressed expected shortfall and liquidity horizons of 20 to 120 days. The 99.9% one-year VaR applies to jump-to-default risk.
cards.originalText: Credit spread risk.
cards.correction: Under the FRTB internal models approach, jump-to-default risk has a capital charge based on a 99.9% VaR with a one-year horizon.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to market risk capital.
cards.explanation: Trading book instruments attract market risk capital, whereas banking book instruments attract credit risk capital.
cards.originalText: Market risk capital

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to credit risk capital.
cards.explanation: Credit risk capital applies to banking book instruments. Trading book instruments are subject to market risk capital.
cards.originalText: Credit risk capital
cards.correction: Under the FRTB, instruments in the trading book are subject to market risk capital.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, banks must use the standardized approach to compute capital for securitizations such as asset-backed securities and collateralized debt obligations.
cards.explanation: Model-based securitization charges varied widely across banks for the same portfolio, so the FRTB mandates the standardized approach for securitizations.
cards.originalText: The standardized approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, banks may use the internal models approach based on expected shortfall to compute capital for securitizations.
cards.explanation: The internal models approach is not permitted for securitizations under the FRTB, which requires the standardized approach.
cards.originalText: The internal models approach (IMA) using expected shortfall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.loText: Explain the FRTB revisions to Basel regulations in the following areas: - Classification of positions in the trading book compared to the banking book. - Backtesting, profit and loss attribution, credit risk, and securitizations.
cards.reading: MR-18: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
cards.statement: Under the FRTB, capital for securitizations is computed with the comprehensive risk measure using the bank's own internal model.
cards.explanation: The comprehensive risk measure was the Basel II.5 internal-model charge. The FRTB replaced it for securitizations with the standardized approach because of the variation in results across banks.
cards.originalText: The comprehensive risk measure (CRM) using the bank’s own internal model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
cards.statement: Under bootstrapped historical simulation, each resample is drawn from the observed data with replacement, the best VaR estimate is the mean of the resample VaRs, and each resample ES is the average of the losses beyond that resample's VaR.
cards.explanation: A bootstrap resamples the existing data set with replacement. Each resample gives a VaR and ES, and the best estimate is the mean of the resample-based estimates.
cards.originalText: Under bootstrapped HS, each resample is drawn from the 500 observations with replacement, the best VaR estimate is the mean of the resample VaRs, and each resample ES is the average of the losses beyond that resample’s VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
cards.statement: Under volatility-weighted historical simulation, historical returns are scaled down when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day on which the return was observed.
