cards.explanation: Returns are scaled up when current volatility is higher than the volatility forecast at the time of the observation, and scaled down when it is lower. The adjustment multiplies by the ratio of current to historical volatility.
cards.originalText: Under volatility-weighted HS, the −3.0% return enters the adjusted series as −2.25%, because historical returns are scaled down when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day they were observed.
cards.correction: Under volatility-weighted historical simulation, historical returns are scaled up when the current volatility forecast is above the forecast for the day on which the return was observed.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
cards.statement: Filtered historical simulation produces VaR and ES estimates that cannot exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.
cards.explanation: Like volatility-weighted historical simulation, filtered historical simulation rescales returns by current volatility and can produce VaR and ES estimates larger than the maximum historical loss. That cap applies to basic historical simulation.
cards.originalText: Under filtered HS, the standardised return of −2.5 is bootstrapped and rescaled by the 1.6% forecast to −4.0%, but the resulting VaR and ES still cannot exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.
cards.correction: Filtered historical simulation can produce VaR and ES estimates that exceed the largest loss in the historical sample.

changes.from: produces VaR and ES estimates that cannot exceed
changes.to: can produce VaR and ES estimates that exceed

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
cards.statement: The standard bootstrap procedure remains reliable when returns are dependent over time, because each observation is drawn at random from the full window.
cards.explanation: Standard bootstrap procedures presuppose that observations are independent over time. With dependent returns, remedies include bootstrapping GARCH residuals or using block bootstraps.
cards.originalText: Under bootstrapped HS, the standard resampling procedure remains reliable when returns are dependent over time, because each observation is drawn at random from the full window of 500 observations.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the age-weighted, the volatility-weighted, the correlation-weighted, and the filtered historical simulation approaches.
cards.statement: Expected shortfall is subadditive, so the combined ES of two portfolios cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone ESs, and filtered historical simulation can be extended to estimate ES.
cards.explanation: ES is a coherent risk measure and satisfies subadditivity. Filtered historical simulation can be used to estimate ES as well as VaR.
cards.originalText: Because ES is subadditive, the combined ES of the two desks cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone ESs, and FHS can be extended to estimate ES.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the age-weighted, the volatility-weighted, the correlation-weighted, and the filtered historical simulation approaches.
cards.statement: Because VaR is subadditive for skewed loss distributions, the combined 99% VaR of two portfolios cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone VaRs.
cards.explanation: VaR is subadditive for elliptical distributions such as the normal. Non-subadditivity can occur when portfolios have very skewed loss distributions, so merging skewed portfolios can make combined VaR exceed the sum.
cards.originalText: Because VaR is subadditive for skewed loss distributions, the combined 99% VaR of the two desks cannot exceed the sum of their stand-alone VaRs.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the age-weighted, the volatility-weighted, the correlation-weighted, and the filtered historical simulation approaches.
cards.statement: Because expected shortfall averages all tail losses, its estimators have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, and the advantage grows as tails become heavier.
cards.explanation: ES estimators tend to have bigger standard errors than VaR estimators for heavy-tailed distributions, because ES is more prone to large but infrequent losses.
cards.originalText: Because ES averages all tail losses, its estimators have smaller standard errors than VaR estimators, and the advantage grows as tails become heavier.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Given model risk, choosing the Frechet case for extreme value analysis is the conservative choice, because extreme value risk measures rise with the tail index and wrongly concluding $\xi = 0$ would understate extreme risk.
cards.explanation: One way of choosing between the extreme value cases is to always choose the Frechet, since a test that cannot reject $\xi = 0$ leaves the analyst open to understating extreme risk.
cards.originalText: Given model risk, and since EV risk measures rise with the tail index, the conservative choice is the Frechet case, because wrongly concluding $\xi= 0$ would understate extreme risk.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Because a tail index estimate is not significantly different from zero, adopting the Gumbel case can only overstate, never understate, extreme risk measures.
cards.explanation: Extreme value risk measures rise with the tail index, so wrongly accepting $\xi = 0$ understates extreme risk.
cards.originalText: Because $\xi$ is not significantly different from zero, the Gumbel case should be adopted, since accepting $\xi= 0$ can only overstate, never understate, the extreme risk measures.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: If the parent loss distribution is a Student's $t$, the Gumbel case is appropriate because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution.
cards.explanation: The Student's $t$ distribution has heavy power-law tails and lies in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution, not the Gumbel.
cards.originalText: If the parent loss distribution is believed to be a Student’s $t$, the Gumbel case is appropriate, because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution.
cards.correction: If the parent loss distribution is a Student's $t$, the Frechet case is appropriate because the $t$ lies in the domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution.

changes.from: domain of attraction of the Gumbel distribution
changes.to: domain of attraction of the Frechet distribution

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: The block maxima approach needs no threshold choice but can waste useful data because a block may contain more than one extreme loss, whereas the peaks-over-threshold approach models all losses above a high threshold.
cards.explanation: Block maxima keeps only the largest loss in each block, so extra extreme losses in the same block are discarded. Peaks over threshold uses every loss above the chosen threshold.
cards.originalText: The block maxima approach needs no threshold choice, but it can waste useful data because a quarter may contain more than one extreme loss; the peaks-over-threshold approach models all losses above a high threshold.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: The block maxima approach fits a two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution to the largest loss in each block, so it needs fewer parameters than the peaks-over-threshold approach.
cards.explanation: The two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution belongs to peaks over threshold. The GEV distribution fitted to block maxima has three parameters: location, scale and tail index.
cards.originalText: The block maxima approach fits a two-parameter generalised Pareto distribution to the largest loss in each quarter, so it needs fewer parameters than the peaks-over-threshold approach.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: A positive tail index places a fitted GEV distribution in the Weibull case with lighter-than-normal tails.
cards.explanation: A positive tail index is the Frechet case, with heavy power-law tails. The Weibull case, with tails lighter than normal, corresponds to a negative tail index.
cards.originalText: A positive tail index places the fitted GEV in the Weibull case with lighter than normal tails, so a positive estimate signals that extreme losses are less likely than under a normal parent.
cards.correction: A negative tail index places a fitted GEV distribution in the Weibull case with lighter-than-normal tails.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
cards.statement: Because both block maxima and peaks over threshold rest on extreme value theorems, they remain valid for operational losses pooled across business lines and risk types, whatever mechanism produced each loss.
cards.explanation: Extreme value theory is only valid if a single mechanism is responsible for all observed losses. With losses from different business lines and risk types this is unlikely to hold.
cards.originalText: Because both approaches rest on extreme-value theorems, they remain valid for losses pooled across business lines and risk types, whatever mechanism produced each loss.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach models the excess of each loss over a high threshold $u$, conditional on $u$ being exceeded, and does not require the parent loss distribution to be known.
cards.explanation: POT applies extreme value theory to the distribution of excess losses over a threshold. The parent distribution can be any of the commonly used distributions and is usually unknown.
cards.originalText: POT models the excess of each loss over a high threshold $u$, conditional on $u$ being exceeded, and does not require the parent loss distribution to be known.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach fits a distribution to the largest loss in each block of equal length, so it uses one observation per block and needs no threshold.
cards.explanation: Using one maximum per block with no threshold describes the block maxima (GEV) approach. POT models all excesses over a high threshold.
cards.originalText: POT fits a distribution to the largest loss in each block of equal length, so it uses one observation per block and needs no threshold.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: The peaks-over-threshold approach requires the parent loss distribution to be normal or lognormal, because the excess distribution is derived from the parent's parameters.
cards.explanation: The parent distribution can be almost any common distribution and is usually unknown. The generalised Pareto limit for excesses does not require a normal or lognormal parent.
cards.originalText: POT requires the parent loss distribution to be normal or lognormal, because the excess distribution is derived from the parent’s parameters.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, $F(u)$ is naturally estimated by the proportion of losses that do not exceed the threshold, because the generalised Pareto fit describes losses only conditional on exceeding $u$.
cards.explanation: The GP fit gives the distribution of excesses over $u$. To obtain the unconditional tail, $F(x) = (1 - F(u))G(x - u) + F(u)$, the share of losses at or below $u$ must be supplied separately from the data.
cards.originalText: 1,940/2,000 = 97%, the share of losses not exceeding $u$, because the GP fit describes losses only conditional on exceeding $u$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the natural estimator of $F(u)$ is the proportion of losses that exceed the threshold.
cards.explanation: The proportion of exceedances estimates $1 - F(u)$. $F(u)$ itself is estimated by the proportion of losses not exceeding the threshold.
cards.originalText: 60/2,000 = 3%, the share of exceedances, because $F (u)$ is the probability that a loss exceeds the threshold.
cards.correction: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the natural estimator of $F(u)$ is the proportion of losses that do not exceed the threshold.

changes.to: that do not exceed the threshold

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold $u$ can be estimated by maximum likelihood together with the generalised Pareto parameters, which makes the threshold an objective output of the fit.
cards.explanation: Maximum likelihood estimates $\beta$ and $\xi$ given a threshold. The choice of $u$ remains inevitably arbitrary and judgemental.
cards.originalText: Estimate $u$ by maximum likelihood together with $\beta$ and $\xi$, which makes the threshold an objective output of the fitting procedure.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold should be set equal to the target 99.9% VaR so that the generalised Pareto distribution is fitted to exactly the losses that define the VaR.
cards.explanation: A threshold at the 99.9% VaR leaves very few exceedances, too few to estimate the parameters, and is circular because the VaR is the quantity being estimated.
cards.originalText: Set $u$ equal to the target 99.9% VaR, so that the GP distribution is fitted to exactly the 0.1% of losses that define the VaR.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: In the peaks-over-threshold approach, the threshold should be set as low as possible, because the GPBdH theorem holds at any threshold once the number of exceedances is large.
cards.explanation: The GPBdH theorem holds as the threshold becomes large. Lowering the threshold to gather more data adds bias.
cards.originalText: Set $u$ as low as possible, because the GPBdH theorem holds at any threshold once the number of exceedances is large.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis increases the number of exceedances and lowers the variance of the estimates, but adds bias because more exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
cards.explanation: There is a bias-variance trade-off: a lower threshold gives more data and a smaller variance, but the extra observations are less extreme and so the GP approximation is less accurate.
cards.originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% raises the number of exceedances to 150 and lowers the variance of the estimates, but adds bias, because more exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
cards.explanation: The trade-off runs the other way: more exceedances from nearer the centre lower the variance of the estimates but raise the bias.
cards.originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.
cards.correction: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis raises the bias of the estimates but lowers their variance, because the additional exceedances come from closer to the centre of the distribution.

changes.from: reduces the bias of the estimates but raises their variance
changes.to: raises the bias of the estimates but lowers their variance

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.
cards.statement: Lowering the threshold in a peaks-over-threshold analysis makes the GPBdH approximation more accurate, because the theorem holds for any threshold that leaves many exceedances.
cards.explanation: The GPBdH theorem holds as the threshold gets large, so lowering the threshold weakens the approximation. The number of exceedances is not the condition.
cards.originalText: Lowering $u$ to 1.2% raises the number of exceedances to 150 and also makes the GPBdH approximation more accurate, because the theorem holds for any threshold that leaves many exceedances.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: By the GPBdH theorem, excess losses over a sufficiently high threshold converge to a generalised Pareto distribution almost regardless of the parent distribution of the losses.
cards.explanation: This limiting result is why the generalised Pareto distribution is the natural model for excess losses, rather than a normal distribution fitted to the same data.
cards.originalText: By the GPBdH theorem, excess losses over a high threshold converge to a GP distribution almost regardless of the parent, and the GP puts more mass in the tail than the normal does.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: By the Fisher-Tippett theorem, excess losses converge to a generalised Pareto distribution only when the parent distribution is normal.
cards.explanation: Fisher-Tippett concerns the distribution of maxima. The GPBdH theorem governs excesses over a threshold and does not require a normal parent.
cards.originalText: By the Fisher-Tippett theorem, excess losses converge to a GP distribution only when the parent is normal, so the GP and the normal give the same tail estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: In a peaks-over-threshold model, a fitted generalised Pareto tail index $\xi > 0$ implies a heavy, power-law tail, and the expected shortfall exists provided $\xi < 1$.
cards.explanation: A positive tail index gives a heavy power-law tail. The POT expected shortfall formula, ES = VaR/(1 − $\xi$) + ($\beta - \xi u$)/(1 − $\xi$), requires $\xi < 1$.
cards.originalText: Because $\xi> 0$, the excess losses have a heavy, power-law tail, and the POT expected shortfall exists because $\xi< 1$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: The tail index $\xi$ of the generalised Pareto distribution is specific to that distribution and has no counterpart in extreme value (GEV) theory.
cards.explanation: The tail index $\xi$ in the generalised Pareto distribution is the same tail index as in GEV theory.
cards.originalText: $\xi$ is a tail index specific to the GP distribution with no counterpart in GEV theory, so it cannot be compared with block maxima estimates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the application of the generalized Pareto (GP) distribution in the POT approach.
cards.statement: In the generalised Pareto distribution used in peaks over threshold, $\beta$ is a location parameter that measures the central tendency of the excess losses.
cards.explanation: $\beta$ is the scale parameter. The generalised Pareto distribution has a scale parameter and a tail index, and no location parameter.
cards.originalText: $\beta$ is a location parameter that measures the central tendency of the excess losses, so it must be estimated together with $u$.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A negative correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen) makes a quanto call on the Nikkei more expensive, because a rising index comes with a falling yen and the seller needs more yen to cover the dollar payoff.
cards.explanation: The quanto seller faces two unknowns: the yen payoff and the exchange rate at which it is converted. A negative correlation between the index and USD per yen makes them move against the seller, so the quanto costs more.
cards.originalText: If the correlation between the Nikkei and $X$ is negative, a rising Nikkei comes with a falling yen, so the seller needs more yen for the dollar payoff and the quanto is more expensive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen), the more expensive a quanto call on the Nikkei.
cards.explanation: The more positive the correlation, the cheaper the quanto: a rising index comes with a rising yen, so fewer yen are needed to meet the dollar payoff.
cards.originalText: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei and $X$, the more expensive the quanto call, because the seller must convert a larger yen payoff.
cards.correction: The more positive the correlation between the Nikkei 225 and the exchange rate (USD per yen), the cheaper a quanto call on the Nikkei.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The seller of a quanto call is uncertain only about the exchange rate at maturity, because the foreign-currency payoff it must convert is fixed at inception.
cards.explanation: The foreign-currency payoff is not fixed. It depends on how deep in the money the call finishes, which is why the product is called a quanto (from quantity).
cards.originalText: The seller of the quanto call is uncertain only about the exchange rate at maturity, because the yen payoff it must convert is fixed at inception.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A basket call option on an equally weighted portfolio of two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
cards.explanation: Lower correlation means more offsetting moves inside the basket, which reduces the basket's volatility and so the value of the call.
cards.originalText: A basket call option on an equally weighted portfolio of the two stocks

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A call on the maximum of two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
cards.explanation: A call on the maximum benefits from dispersion: with lower correlation one stock is more likely to finish high, so its price rises.
cards.originalText: A call on the maximum of the two stocks
cards.correction: A call on the maximum of two stocks becomes more expensive when the correlation between the stocks falls.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe how correlation impacts the price of quanto options as well as other multi-asset exotic options.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A spread call option on the difference between two stocks becomes cheaper when the correlation between the stocks falls.
cards.explanation: A spread option is priced off the volatility of the difference, $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}$, which rises as $\rho$ falls, so the option becomes more expensive.
cards.originalText: A spread call option on the difference between the two stocks
cards.correction: A spread call option on the difference between two stocks becomes more expensive when the correlation between the stocks falls.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Paying the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a stock market sell-off, because correlations between stocks typically rise when stock prices fall.
cards.explanation: The fixed-rate payer is long correlation and receives $N(\rho_{realised} - \rho_{fixed})$, which gains when correlations jump in a downturn.
cards.originalText: Paying the fixed rate in a correlation swap on the fund’s main holdings indirectly hedges a sell-off, because correlations between stocks typically rise when stock prices fall.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Receiving the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a stock market sell-off, because realised correlation falls in a downturn.
cards.explanation: The fixed-rate receiver is short correlation and loses when realised correlation rises, which is what typically happens in a sell-off. The payer is the one hedged.
cards.originalText: Receiving the fixed rate in a correlation swap indirectly hedges a sell-off, because the fund locks in a known correlation while realised correlation falls in a downturn.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Buying put options on individual stocks and selling put options on the index is a way of buying correlation.
cards.explanation: Buying correlation with options means being long index options and short single-stock options, because index volatility rises with correlation. The legs in the statement are reversed.
cards.originalText: Buying put options on the individual stocks and selling put options on the index is a way of buying correlation, because index volatility rises with correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: A correlation swap can be valued with standard swap techniques, because traders can bootstrap a market-implied term structure of correlation.
cards.explanation: There is no industry-standard valuation model and no market term structure of correlation. Traders use historical data or stochastic correlation models.
cards.originalText: The swap can be valued with standard swap techniques, because traders can bootstrap a market-implied term structure of correlation.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: In 2012 the London Whale sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and bought CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if volatility and correlation fell in a recovering economy.
cards.explanation: Selling index protection and buying single-name protection is a short-correlation position in credit. In a recovering economy volatility and correlation typically decrease.
cards.originalText: In 2012 the “London Whale” sold CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and bought CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if volatility and correlation fell in a recovering economy.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: In 2012 the London Whale bought CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and sold CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if correlation rose in a recovering economy.
cards.explanation: The trade was the mirror image: index protection was sold and single-name protection bought, with the expectation that correlation would fall.
cards.originalText: In 2012 the “London Whale” bought CDS on the CDX.NA.IG.9 index and sold CDS on individual names, a position expected to profit if correlation rose in a recovering economy.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Correlation swaps are valued with an industry-standard model that discounts the fixed leg off a market term structure of correlation.
cards.explanation: There is no industry-standard valuation model and no market term structure of correlation. Traders rely on historical data or stochastic correlation models.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: The present value of a correlation swap rises for the fixed-rate receiver when realised correlation increases during the life of the swap.
cards.explanation: Rising realised correlation raises the value for the fixed-rate payer, who receives realised minus fixed correlation. It lowers the value for the fixed-rate receiver.
cards.correction: The present value of a correlation swap rises for the fixed-rate payer when realised correlation increases during the life of the swap.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: For two borrowers that each have a 10% default probability, a default correlation of −0.1 leaves the joint default probability positive, at about 0.1%.
cards.explanation: Joint PD = $\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y + P_X P_Y = -0.1 \times 0.3 \times 0.3 + 0.01 = 0.1\%$. A slightly negative correlation does not eliminate the joint default.
cards.originalText: With a default correlation of −0.1 the joint default probability is still positive, at about 0.1%, so a slightly negative correlation does not eliminate the worst case.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: With any negative default correlation between two borrowers, the joint default probability is zero.
cards.explanation: The joint default probability stays positive until the correlation is sufficiently negative (about −0.111 for two 10% borrowers). Only then does it reach zero.
cards.originalText: With any negative default correlation the joint default probability is zero, so a negatively correlated pair removes the worst case entirely.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: With a default correlation of 1, splitting one loan into two equal loans to different borrowers halves the worst-case probability of loss.
cards.explanation: At a correlation of 1 the loans default together or survive together, so the worst-case probability is unchanged and diversification brings no benefit.
cards.originalText: With a default correlation of 1, splitting one loan into these two equal loans halves the worst-case probability from 10% to 5%.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.loText: Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.
cards.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
cards.statement: Lending to two borrowers in the same sector reduces concentration risk more than lending across sectors, because intra-sector default correlations are lower.
cards.explanation: Default correlations are higher within a sector, so lending across sectors diversifies more.
cards.correction: Lending across sectors reduces concentration risk more than lending to two borrowers in the same sector, because intra-sector default correlations are higher.

changes.from: Lending to two borrowers in the same sector reduces concentration risk more than lending across sectors
changes.to: Lending across sectors reduces concentration risk more than lending to two borrowers in the same sector

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: When an arbitrage-free model such as Ho-Lee is fitted to prices distorted by a temporary liquidity effect, such as a forced liquidation, it attributes that liquidity effect to the interest rate process.
cards.explanation: The fitted drift treats the distorted swap prices as fair. The prices are fair given the liquidation, not fair with respect to expected rates and the risk premium.
cards.originalText: Fitting to the distorted prices attributes a liquidity effect to the interest rate process; the 7-year swaps are fair given the liquidation, not fair with respect to expected rates and the risk premium.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Because the Ho-Lee model is arbitrage-free, its recalibrated prices are fair values and its hedges remain accurate by construction.
cards.explanation: Matching market prices does not make them fair values or guarantee accurate hedges. If market prices are distorted, an arbitrage-free model inherits the distortion.
cards.originalText: Because Ho-Lee is arbitrage-free, its recalibrated prices are fair values and its hedges remain accurate by construction.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The Ho-Lee drift can be chosen to match all input spot rates, but the model remains a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.
cards.explanation: The time-dependent drift fits the spot rate curve, but volatility is a constant $\sigma$ and shocks move all rates equally.
cards.originalText: The Ho-Lee drift can match all input spot rates, but the model remains a parallel-shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Because its drift varies with time, the Ho-Lee model produces a humped term structure of volatility that matches market implied volatilities.
cards.explanation: In Ho-Lee the drift has no effect on the shape of the volatility structure, which is flat. A humped volatility structure is a feature of models such as Gauss+.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Because the drift $\lambda(t)$ is calibrated to market spot rates, the Ho-Lee model rules out negative short-term rates.
cards.explanation: Calibrating the drift fits prices but leaves rates normally distributed, so negative rates remain possible.
cards.originalText: Because $\lambda(t)$ is calibrated to market spot rates, the Ho-Lee model rules out negative short-term rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe uses and benefits of the arbitrage-free models and assess the issue of fitting models to market prices.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: The exponentially decaying volatility in Model 3 introduces mean reversion, so Model 3 is no longer a parallel-shift model.
cards.explanation: Model 3 has time-dependent volatility but no mean reversion, so it remains a parallel-shift model.
cards.originalText: The exponential decay in Model 3’s volatility introduces mean reversion, so Model 3 is no longer a parallel-shift model.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the CIR model, basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the short rate and falls to zero when the rate is zero, where the drift is positive, which keeps the rate from becoming negative.
cards.explanation: CIR volatility is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ with mean reversion, so it rises with the rate but less than proportionally and vanishes at a zero rate, where the positive drift pushes the rate back up.
cards.originalText: The CIR model, because its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate and falls to zero at a zero rate, where the drift is positive.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: Mean reversion in the Vasicek model prevents the short rate from becoming negative.
cards.explanation: Vasicek has constant basis-point volatility and normally distributed rates, so negative rates remain possible despite mean reversion.
cards.originalText: The Vasicek model, because mean reversion pulls the short rate toward its long-run level and therefore prevents the short rate from becoming negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Black-Karasinski model, basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the short rate.
cards.explanation: Black-Karasinski is lognormal, so its basis-point volatility is proportional to the rate. The square-root dependence is a CIR property.
cards.originalText: The Black-Karasinski model, because the logarithm of the rate mean-reverts and its basis-point volatility rises with the square root of the rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.loText: Describe the process of constructing a simple and recombining tree for a short-term rate under the Vasicek Model with mean reversion.
cards.reading: MR-14: The Art of Term Structure Models: Drift
cards.statement: In the Ho-Lee model, fitting the time-dependent drift to market bond prices guarantees that no node of the rate tree becomes negative.
cards.explanation: Ho-Lee rates are normally distributed with constant volatility. Fitting the drift matches bond prices but does not prevent low nodes from going negative.
cards.originalText: The Ho-Lee model, because fitting its time-dependent drift to market bond prices guarantees that no node of the rate tree becomes negative.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, the term structure of volatility is flat at any given date, but its level declines over time as $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ falls.
cards.explanation: Model 3 changes only the volatility term, which depends on calendar time. At any date all rates still shift in parallel, so volatility is flat across maturities, but the level falls over time.
cards.originalText: At any given date the term structure of volatility is flat, but its level changes over time as $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ declines.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, produces non-parallel shifts because its volatility decays over time.
cards.explanation: Without mean reversion, shocks move all rates equally. Non-parallel shifts require mean reversion, as in the Vasicek model.
cards.originalText: Because volatility decays over time, a shock to the short rate now moves short-term rates more than long-term rates, so Model 3 produces non-parallel shifts.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, basis-point volatility depends on the level of the short rate, which prevents negative rates.
cards.explanation: Model 3 volatility depends on calendar time, not on the level of the rate, and rates remain normally distributed, so negative rates are still possible.
cards.originalText: Because volatility now depends on the level of the short rate, basis-point volatility falls when rates fall, which prevents negative rates.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: Setting $\alpha = 0$ turns Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, into the Vasicek model with constant volatility.
cards.explanation: With $\alpha = 0$ the volatility is a constant $\sigma$ and the drift is still $\lambda(t)$, which is the Ho-Lee model. Vasicek requires a mean-reverting drift $k(\theta - r)$.
cards.originalText: Setting $\alpha= 0$ turns Model 3 into the Vasicek model with constant volatility.
cards.correction: Setting $\alpha = 0$ turns Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, into the Ho-Lee model with constant volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: If Model 3 is given an initial volatility and decay rate equal to Vasicek's $\sigma$ and $k$, with a time-dependent drift matching the average Vasicek path, the two models have identical terminal distributions of the short rate, yet Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model while Vasicek does not.
cards.explanation: The terminal standard deviations and means can be matched, so the terminal distributions coincide. Curve dynamics still differ, because only Vasicek has mean reversion and therefore non-parallel shifts.
cards.originalText: The two models produce identical terminal distributions of the short rate, yet Model 3 remains a parallel-shift model while Vasicek does not.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: If two short-rate models have identical terminal distributions of the short rate, they imply identical yield curve shifts and therefore identical hedge ratios.
cards.explanation: Identical terminal distributions do not imply identical curve dynamics. For example, a Model 3 can match Vasicek's terminal distribution while shifting in parallel, whereas Vasicek does not.
cards.originalText: Because the terminal distributions are identical, the two models imply identical yield curve shifts and therefore identical hedge ratios.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.loText: Calculate the short-term rate change and determine the behavior of the standard deviation of the rate change using a model with time-dependent volatility.
cards.reading: MR-15: The Art of Term Structure Models: Volatility and Distribution
cards.statement: In Model 3, $dr = \lambda(t)dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}dw$, the standard deviation of the terminal distribution of the short rate declines toward zero as the horizon lengthens, because the instantaneous volatility decays to zero.
cards.explanation: The instantaneous volatility declines, but the terminal standard deviation accumulates the variance of every step from today to $T$, so it can only rise with the horizon (at a decreasing rate).
cards.originalText: It declines toward zero, because the volatility $\sigma\text{e}^{-\alpha t}$ decays to zero.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model has three state variables but only two sources of risk, because the short-term rate has no random shock of its own.
cards.explanation: The state is described by $r$, $m$ and $l$, but only $dW^1$ and $dW^2$ appear in the dynamics, and $dr$ has no random term.
cards.originalText: The model has three state variables but only two sources of risk, because the short-term rate has no random shock of its own.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Gauss+ model has three sources of risk, one for each of the short rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor.
cards.explanation: There are only two sources of risk. The "+" marks a state variable that is not itself a source of risk, because the short rate has no shock of its own.
cards.originalText: The model has three sources of risk, one for each of $r$, $m$ and $l$, and the “+” in its name refers to this third source.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: Rates in the Gauss+ model are lognormally distributed, which keeps the short-term rate above zero at all horizons.
cards.explanation: "Gauss" means rates are normally distributed, so negative rates are possible.
cards.originalText: Rates are lognormally distributed in Gauss+, which keeps the short-term rate above zero at all horizons.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_r$ makes changes in the factors $m$ and $l$ pass into the term structure of rates faster.
cards.explanation: The short rate reverts to $m$ at speed $\alpha_r$. The faster it does so, the sooner changes in $m$ and, through $m$, in $l$ show up in short rates and the whole term structure.
cards.originalText: A larger $\alpha_{r}$ makes changes in the factors $m$ and $l$ make their way into the term structure of rates faster.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_m$ makes $m$ converge to $l$ more slowly and increases the effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.
cards.explanation: A larger $\alpha_m$ means faster convergence of $m$ to $l$ and a smaller effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.
cards.originalText: A larger $\alpha_{m}$ makes $m$ converge to $l$ more slowly and increases the effect of $m$ on longer-term yields.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Describe the structure of the Gauss+ model and discuss the implications of this structure for the model’s ability to replicate empirically observed interest rate dynamics.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_l$ lengthens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ persist longer.
cards.explanation: Half-life is $\ln 2/\alpha_l$, which falls as $\alpha_l$ rises, so shocks to $l$ die out faster.
cards.originalText: A larger $\alpha_{l}$ lengthens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ persist longer.
cards.correction: In the Gauss+ model, a larger $\alpha_l$ shortens the half-life of the long-term factor, so shocks to $l$ die out faster.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: The Vasicek model can reasonably be used to price, compare values and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years.
cards.explanation: Vasicek can be calibrated to match 10- to 30-year noncallable bonds and the 10-year rate volatility, which suits long-term bonds callable after an intermediate period.
cards.originalText: Using Vasicek to price, compare and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years, calibrated to match 10- to 30-year noncallable bonds and the 10-year rate volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.topic: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.loText: Compare and contrast the dynamics, features, and applications of the Vasicek model and the Gauss+ model.
cards.reading: MR-16: The Vasicek and Gauss+ Models
cards.statement: Unlike the Vasicek model, the Gauss+ model adds a random shock to the short-term rate.
cards.explanation: The reverse is true: Vasicek has a random shock on the short rate, while Gauss+ is defined by the absence of a shock to the short-term rate.
cards.originalText: Using Gauss+ for caps across the curve because, unlike Vasicek, it adds a random shock to the short-term rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: For equity options, implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and when short-dated implied volatilities are historically low, at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
cards.explanation: Equity options show a downward-sloping volatility skew in strike. When short-dated volatility is low relative to its long-run level, the ATM volatility term structure is expected to slope upward.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility falls as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: For equity options, implied volatility rises as the strike price rises.
cards.explanation: For equity options (stocks and stock indices), implied volatility decreases as the strike price increases.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility rises as the strike price rises, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.
cards.correction: For equity options, implied volatility falls as the strike price rises.

changes.from: rises as the strike price rises
changes.to: falls as the strike price rises

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe a volatility smile and volatility skew.
cards.statement: For equity options, implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises toward both lower and higher strikes.
cards.explanation: A U-shaped smile that is lowest at the money describes foreign currency options. Equity options show a downward-sloping skew, with the highest volatilities at low strikes.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises toward both lower and higher strikes, and at-the-money implied volatility is expected to increase with option maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: A European call and put on a non-dividend-paying index with the same strike and maturity gain the same dollar amount in value when implied volatility rises, because $c - p = S_{0} - Ke^{-rT}$ does not depend on volatility.
cards.explanation: By put-call parity the difference between call and put values is independent of volatility, so a change in volatility changes both values by the same amount.
cards.originalText: Both options gain by the same dollar amount, because $c -p = S_{0} -K\text{e}^{-rT}$ does not depend on volatility.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: When implied volatility rises, a European call gains value and a European put with the same strike and maturity loses value, because the two have deltas of opposite sign.
cards.explanation: Both options gain when volatility rises (vega is positive for both). The opposite signs belong to delta, which is the sensitivity to the underlying, not to volatility.
cards.originalText: The call gains and the put loses value, because the two options have deltas of opposite sign.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: When implied volatility rises, a European call gains more value than a European put with the same strike and maturity, because the call's payoff is unlimited on the upside.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity shows that the call-minus-put difference contains no volatility term, so both options gain by the same dollar amount.
cards.originalText: Both options gain value, but the call gains more because its payoff is unlimited on the upside.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: If a European put has a higher implied volatility than a European call with the same strike and maturity on a non-dividend-paying stock, the put is expensive relative to the call, and the arbitrage is to sell the put, buy the call and short the stock, investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity forces a call and a put with the same strike and maturity to share one implied volatility. The option with the higher implied volatility is overpriced, so it is sold and the parity position is completed with the other option and the stock.
cards.originalText: The put is expensive relative to the call, so the trader should sell the put, buy the call and short the stock, investing the proceeds at the risk-free rate.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: No action is needed when a call and a put with the same strike and maturity have different implied volatilities, because the equity skew assigns higher implied volatilities to puts than to calls.
cards.explanation: The skew relates implied volatility to the strike, across strikes. At the same strike and maturity, put-call parity requires the call and put to share one implied volatility, so a difference signals an arbitrage.
cards.originalText: No action is needed, because the equity skew assigns higher implied volatilities to puts than to calls.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of put-call parity on the implied volatility of call and put options.
cards.statement: An arbitrage between a European call and put with the same strike and maturity but different implied volatilities exists only if the stock price is lognormally distributed.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity does not depend on any assumption about the probability distribution of the stock price, so the arbitrage exists whether or not prices are lognormal.
cards.originalText: An arbitrage exists only if the stock price is lognormally distributed, because the implied volatilities come from BSM.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: Pricing European index options with a single lognormal volatility equal to the at-the-money implied volatility prices deep out-of-the-money index puts below their market prices, because the implied distribution has a heavier left tail than the lognormal.
cards.explanation: Equity index options show a skew: the implied left tail is heavier than lognormal, so deep out-of-the-money puts trade at higher implied volatilities than the ATM level.
cards.originalText: Deep out-of-the-money index puts are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier left tail than the lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: Pricing European index options with a single lognormal volatility equal to the at-the-money implied volatility prices deep out-of-the-money index calls below their market prices, because the implied distribution has a heavier right tail than the lognormal.
cards.explanation: The implied distribution of an equity index has a less heavy right tail than the lognormal, so deep OTM calls are priced above market by the lognormal model. A heavier right tail is a currency feature.
cards.originalText: Deep out-of-the-money index calls are priced below market, because the implied distribution has a heavier right tail than the lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Compare the shape of the volatility smile (or skew) to the shape of the implied distribution of the underlying asset price and to the pricing of options on the underlying asset.
cards.statement: If options are priced with a single lognormal volatility, options at every strike are priced at market, because put-call parity forces one implied volatility on every option with the same maturity.
cards.explanation: Put-call parity makes a call and a put with the same strike and maturity share one implied volatility. It does not equalise implied volatilities across strikes, which is why smiles and skews exist.
cards.originalText: Options at every strike are priced at market, because put-call parity forces one implied volatility on every option with the same maturity.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rate distributions are more peaked and have heavier tails than the lognormal, so deep out-of-the-money calls and puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
cards.explanation: Empirically, fewer small moves and more large moves occur than the lognormal predicts. The heavier tails raise the prices of far out-of-the-money options, giving a volatility smile.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: Exchange rate distributions have heavier tails than the lognormal only on the downside, so only deep out-of-the-money puts should trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options.
cards.explanation: Foreign currency distributions have heavy tails on both sides, giving a roughly symmetric smile. A heavy downside tail only is the equity pattern.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: When a central bank credibly commits to keep an exchange rate within a band, implied volatility is highest at the money and lower for strikes near or beyond the band edges, because the band makes both tails thinner than the lognormal.
cards.explanation: A credible band truncates the distribution, so both tails are much thinner than a lognormal with the same ATM volatility. Options struck near or beyond the band edges are therefore worth less and have lower implied volatility.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility is highest at the money and lower for strikes near or beyond 0.97 and 1.03, because the band makes both tails thinner than the lognormal.

cards.subject: Market Risk
cards.loText: Describe characteristics of foreign exchange rate distributions and their implications on option prices and implied volatility.
cards.statement: When a central bank credibly commits to keep an exchange rate within a band, implied volatility is flat across strikes, because the band reduces the volatility of the rate by the same amount at every strike.
cards.explanation: A band changes the shape of the distribution, not just its scale, by thinning both tails. Implied volatility therefore cannot be flat across strikes.
cards.originalText: Implied volatility is flat across strikes, because the band reduces the volatility of the rate by the same amount at every strike.
